a. Estimates are provided below and in CIEC-1 Attachment 1 (Excel, formulas intact) **[TK: Alex Lee: confirm the attachment file name and that it matches the CIEC-1 workbook on Drive]**. The amounts must be read in two parts, because the two groups of customers on Rate HP affect the Company's revenue in completely different ways:

   - _New heat pump customers_ install a heat pump after Rate HP takes effect. As a group, they keep paying their bill from before the heat pump, plus the incremental marginal cost the heat pump causes, so the Company collects more from them than before they installed. They create no shortfall and have no effect on anyone else's rates or bills. ("As a group": Rate HP is calibrated on the average new adopter, so individual customers pay somewhat more or less; see CIEC-13(b).)
   - _Existing heat pump customers_ installed before Rate HP and are auto-enrolled. Their bills fall below the Rate 1 revenue the Company planned to collect from them. This is the only source of any shortfall. Mr. Velez recommends recovering it within the residential class, by setting Rate 1 in this rate case to recover the residential revenue requirement net of Rate HP revenue (CIEC-2(c)).
   - **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** The Company's Rate Year sales forecast already adds winter (Oct–Apr) kWh for heat pumps it expects to install through its C&LM program through 2027.[^1a-clm-forecast] Those forecast adopters are "new" by date, but their heat pump kWh is already in the sales used to set Rate 1, so moving them to Rate HP would lower collections below plan, just like existing customers. The precise line is therefore "heat pump load already in the sales used to set rates" versus "load that is not", not installation date alone. CIEC-12(a) asks exactly this. Proposed fix: in this rate case, move both existing heat pump load and the forecast C&LM heat pump load into Rate HP's billing determinants and recalibrate Rate 1. That cleanly makes "new" mean "beyond the forecast". **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: forecast C&LM heat pump kWh in the Rate Year sales (CLF-SC-001 Attachment 1), and the resulting shortfall at Rate HP's winter rates]**

     [^1a-clm-forecast]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-001](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 ("Adjustments to the sales forecast are made for heat pumps during the heating period for the months of October through April.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-002](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 (adjustments are "based off the 2025-2027 Energy Efficiency Plan").

   - Existing heat pump customer: pays **`{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)`** less per year on Rate HP than on Rate 1, made up of `{python} dollar(c1.dec_dist, 2)` distribution and `{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)` transmission.[^1a-existing-load]

     [^1a-existing-load]: Weighted average of the `{python} num(c1.n_bldg)` buildings in NREL's ResStock 2024.2 building stock model that are assigned to the Company's territory and already heat with a heat pump: `{python} num(c1.annual_kwh)` kWh a year, `{python} num(c1.winter_kwh)` of them in November through March. NREL, _End-Use Load Profiles for the U.S. Building Stock_ (2024), https://doi.org/10.25984/1876417. _See_ CIEC-1 Attachment 1.

   - New heat pump customer: pays **`{python} dollar(c1.new_dec_total, 2)`** less per year than they would pay on Rate 1 after installing (`{python} dollar(c1.new_dec_dist, 2)` distribution, `{python} dollar(c1.new_dec_tx, 2)` transmission). The comparison is to a Rate 1 bill on load the Company never had, so it is lower bills for new customers, not a shortfall.
   - Existing customers, shortfall per year (the same in each of the five years, because the group does not grow): **`{python} million(short_floor['total'])`** at the floor (`{python} num(floor_existing)` customers; `{python} million(short_floor['dist'])` distribution, `{python} million(short_floor['tx'])` transmission) to **`{python} million(short_ceiling['total'])`** at the ceiling (`{python} num(ceiling_existing)` customers; `{python} million(short_ceiling['dist'])` distribution, `{python} million(short_ceiling['tx'])` transmission).
   - Total Rate HP bill reduction relative to Rate 1, both groups, with the split shown:
     - Floor, 2027: `{python} million(floor_2027['total'])` (`{python} million(floor_2027['distribution'])` distribution, `{python} million(floor_2027['transmission'])` transmission), of which the existing-customer shortfall is `{python} million(short_floor['total'])` and lower bills for new customers are `{python} million(floor_2027['total'] - short_floor['total'])`.
     - Floor, 2031: `{python} million(floor_2031['total'])`, of which the shortfall is still `{python} million(short_floor['total'])` and lower bills for new customers are `{python} million(floor_2031['total'] - short_floor['total'])`.

     - Every year, distribution and transmission, both bounds: CIEC-1 Attachment 1.

## CIEC-2

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 95, lines 1-16, and page 98, lines 10-18.


a. Please confirm that Rate HP is not designed to be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole.
b. Please identify who Mr. Velez contends should bear any reduction in distribution and transmission revenue resulting from Rate HP (_e.g._, other residential customers, non-residential customers, or the Company’s shareholders), and explain the basis for that position.
c. Does Mr. Velez recommend that any portion of the revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP be recovered from customers outside the residential class? If so, identify each class and the amount. If not, explain how his recommendations would prevent that result.
d. In developing his recommendations, did Mr. Velez consider how any revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP would be recovered between rate cases through the Company’s reconciling mechanisms? If so, describe that consideration and provide any analysis. If not, explain why not.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Confirmed, with a clarification. Rate HP by itself collects less from heat pump customers than Rate 1 would, so it is not revenue neutral on its own.[^2a-less] It is one of two residential rates. Mr. Velez recommends that Rate 1 be set in this rate case to recover the residential class's revenue requirement net of what Rate HP collects (CIEC-15(b)), so that the residential class as a whole recovers its revenue requirement.

   [^2a-less]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 95:2–4, 95:17–21 (Oct. 21, 2026) (Rate HP is designed so that "every heat pump customer pays less than they would under Rate 1") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Whether there is any reduction to recover depends on who enrolls, as set out in CIEC-1(a):
     - _New heat pump customers:_ as a group, they pay more on Rate HP than before they installed. They reduce no one's revenue and require no recovery from anyone.
     - _Existing heat pump customers:_ they pay `{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)` a year less on Rate HP than on Rate 1 (average). This is the only revenue reduction: `{python} million(short_floor['total'])` to `{python} million(short_ceiling['total'])` a year at the floor and ceiling enrollment estimates.

b. Other residential customers, and only for the existing heat pump customers' reduction.

   - New heat pump customers: no one bears anything (part (a)).
   - Existing heat pump customers' reduction: residential customers not on Rate HP, through Rate 1's distribution and transmission rates. The increase is in CIEC-3(c).
   - Basis: the cross-subsidy the testimony identifies runs within the residential class, from heat pump customers to fossil fuel-heated residential customers (CIEC-16(a)).[^2b-within] Removing it returns the excess to the customers who were receiving it; it does not create a new cost for anyone else.

     [^2b-within]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 5:10–13 (the cross-subsidy "flows from electric customers that heat with heat pumps to those that heat with fossil fuels") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Not non-residential customers: their share of the revenue requirement is set by the class cost allocation, which Rate HP does not change (CIEC-16(b)).
   - Not the Company's shareholders: the overpayment is an allocation problem within the residential class, not evidence that the Company's revenue requirement is too high.

c. No. Mr. Velez recommends that no portion be recovered from customers outside the residential class, and three steps to prevent it:

   1. In this rate case, set Rate 1 and Rate HP using billing determinants that place existing heat pump customers' load on Rate HP, so the existing-customer reduction is built into residential rates rather than appearing later as a shortfall (CIEC-15(b); the resulting Rate 1 rates are in CIEC-3(c)).
   2. Between rate cases, keep any difference caused by Rate HP within the residential class (part (d)).
   3. Set Rate HP's winter Transmission Service Rate within the residential class's transmission revenue requirement, as the Company already does for its own residential rate designs (CIEC-7(d)).[^2c-tsr]

      [^2c-tsr]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-032](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (a winter transmission discount "would require an increase to the first block and non-winter second block rates, to achieve a design equivalent to meet total transmission revenue requirements for the class") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - The Company makes the same commitment for its own Rate 6.[^2c-rate6]

     [^2c-rate6]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 37:18 (July 14, 2026) (Rate 6 "Ensures no incremental harm to remaining customer classes") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

d. Not in the testimony; the testimony does not address the reconciling mechanisms. Mr. Velez has considered them for this response.

   - Decoupling: the Revenue Decoupling Mechanism reconciles the Company's actual distribution revenue to a single company-wide target, at a flat rate per kWh across all classes.[^2d-rdm] Any distribution under- or over-collection is therefore shared by all classes in proportion to their kWh, roughly `{python} pct(nonres_kwh_share)` to non-residential classes on the Rate Year forecast.[^2d-nonres-share]

     [^2d-rdm]: Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 22:21 ("the rate will be set at a flat kWh rate across all rate classes") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f].

     [^2d-nonres-share]: One minus the residential share of Rate Year billed sales: Rate 1 (`{python} num(CLASS_BILLED_MWH)` MWh), Rate 5 (`{python} num(RATE5_MWH)` MWh) and Rate 7 (`{python} num(RATE7_MWH)` MWh), out of `{python} num(RDM_TOTAL_MWH)` MWh for the Company. Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibits CLP-RATES-2.4 and CLP-RATES-2.12 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g] **[TK: pinpoints and public copy; the CLP-RATES-2 extract has no page markers and omits CLP-RATES-2.12]**.

   - Transmission: the Transmission Adjustment Clause is fully reconciling. Class transmission rates are set from each class's allocated share of transmission cost, but the reconciliation is computed for the Company as a whole.[^2d-tac] In the 2023 annual review, for example, the Authority found a single company-wide 2022 over-collection of \$4,603,708 and carried it into the TAC balance.[^2d-tac-2023] Mr. Velez has not found how the carried-forward balance is divided among classes.

     [^2d-tac]: Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-3 at 409 (the clause recovers "the difference between the Company’s TAC revenue and the Company’s TAC costs from the prior period") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

     [^2d-tac-2023]: Docket No. 23-01-03, _PURA Annual Review of the Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company_, [Decision](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/dockcurr.nsf/4b3c728dd1c0d642852586db0069aa70/2458b17f1ae4f1de85258a0d00503765/%24FILE/230103-081623.pdf), at 14–15 (Aug. 16, 2023) (the Company "over-collected 2022 TAC revenue in the amount of \$4,603,708," and "[t]he 2022 over-collection shall be reflected in the carry forward TAC balance") **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - Consequences, if the existing-customer reduction is built into rates in this case (part (c), step 1): no reconciliation shortfall arises from it. Between rate cases, the reconciling mechanisms would see only differences from what was built in:
     - _New heat pump customers:_ as a group, they raise the Company's revenue above what it was before they installed (by about `{python} dollar(c13.mean_bill_delta)` a year each in T&D), producing a small over-collection credited to all classes.
     - _Existing heat pump customers enrolled beyond the number built into rates:_ each lowers distribution revenue by `{python} dollar(c1.dec_dist, 2)` a year, and under the RDM as filed about `{python} pct(nonres_kwh_share)` of that would fall on non-residential classes.
   - Mr. Velez therefore recommends that the Authority direct the Company to (1) report Rate HP customers' billed revenue against what they would have paid on Rate 1, as Massachusetts requires in its decoupling filings,[^2d-ma-report] and (2) recover any shortfall attributable to existing heat pump customers enrolled beyond the number built into rates from the residential class only, for example through a residential-only adjustment or the RDM Rider's provision excluding revenue the Authority approves for exclusion.[^2d-rdm-exclusion]

     [^2d-ma-report]: D.P.U. 25-08-A, Order on Seasonal Heat Pump Rates, at 41 (June 1, 2026) (directing the companies to report "the billed revenues recorded from heat pump customers in their annual revenue decoupling filings and to compare those revenues to the amounts that would have been billed if those customers had not enrolled in the heat pump rates") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026] **[TK: case caption; no public copy to link yet]**.

     [^2d-rdm-exclusion]: Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-3 at 404 (excluding revenue "specifically identified and approved for exclusion by PURA") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

   - The Company's Rate 6 raises the same question. Its worksheet prices Rate 6 on Rate 1's billing determinants and applies a winter discount to the second block, with no line recovering the discount elsewhere.[^2d-rate6-worksheet] So any revenue Rate 6 forgoes relative to Rate 1 between rate cases would also flow through the RDM.

     [^2d-rate6-worksheet]: Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-6 at 2:19–27 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026i].

   - In 2023 the Authority said it was inclined to make the RDM reflect cost causation among classes, but did not plan to keep each class's over- or under-collection within that class, because of rate shock.[^2d-rdm-2023]

     [^2d-rdm-2023]: Docket No. 23-01-03 Decision at 30–31 (inclined to make the RDM "better reflect the underlying cost causation principles relied upon to allocate base distribution costs amongst customers classes," but not planning "to explore an approach that would maintain any over- or under-collection of base distribution revenues within a given customer class") **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - In December 2025 the Authority kept the kWh allocator, after reviewing Company analyses that assigned each class's over- and under-recoveries back to that class, and that split them between residential and commercial and industrial customers.[^2d-rdm-2025]

     [^2d-rdm-2025]: Docket No. 24-12-05, _PURA Procedural Review of the Annual Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company and The United Illuminating Company_, [Decision](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/dockcurr.nsf/4b3c728dd1c0d642852586db0069aa70/27c546791b13210c85258d5c00529872/%24FILE/241205-121025.pdf), at 22 (Dec. 10, 2025) (the class-by-class analysis "indicated significant potential swings to the volumetric rate for certain rate classes that would constitute extreme rate fluctuation"; the residential versus commercial and industrial split "flattened the effects but failed to support an equitable allocator for the RDM revenue requirement"; "at this time, the current allocation methodology used for the RDM is appropriate") **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - The adjustment recommended here is different and narrow: not class-by-class tracking of all revenue variances, but one identifiable amount, attributable to one rate, assigned to the class that rate serves. It cannot produce the swings the Authority was concerned about, because it is bounded by the number of existing heat pump customers enrolled beyond the number built into rates. The statute leaves the choice of decoupling method to the Authority.[^2d-statute]

     [^2d-statute]: [Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-19tt(b)](https://www.cga.ct.gov/current/pub/chap_277.htm#sec_16-19tt) ("The authority shall have the discretion to determine the decoupling mechanism and methodology used in decoupling orders made pursuant to this subsection…").

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** The December 2025 decision (24-12-05 Decision at 22) is adverse to recommendation (2): the Authority looked at a residential versus commercial and industrial split of the RDM and kept the company-wide kWh allocator. CIEC will likely cite it. I've distinguished it above (one bounded amount from one rate, not all variances), but this makes step 1 of part (c), building the existing-customer reduction into this case's rates, the load-bearing remedy, and recommendation (2) a fallback. Do you want to keep (2), soften it to "the Authority could," or drop it and rely on step 1 plus reporting? **[COUNSEL: whether to cite an adverse decision we distinguish, or leave it for CIEC to raise]**

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** The counterfactual problem, which CIEC-6(b) is probably aimed at. Today, when heat pump load grows faster than the rate case forecast, the extra Rate 1 revenue (including the overpayment) is credited back to _all_ classes through the RDM; the Authority itself said beneficial electrification "will result in increased kWh sales and a net RDM credit to customers," and that changing the RDM's allocation "will impact the magnitude of the benefits of beneficial electrification conferred to specific customers and customer class but does not impact the overall or average benefits provided to ratepayers" (23-01-03 Decision at 30, 31 n.19) [NOT INGESTED]. So between rate cases, non-residential customers currently receive about `{python} pct(nonres_kwh_share)` of heat pump customers' overpayment on load beyond the forecast. Rate HP shrinks that credit. Compared with no heat pumps, non-residential customers are no worse off; compared with heat pump adoption on Rate 1, they forgo part of a credit. Options: (1) say so plainly and call that credit what it is, a share of the cross-subsidy that has been flowing across classes, which Rate HP stops; (2) say nothing beyond "relative to no adoption." Option 1 is honest and, I think, persuasive to the Authority, but CIEC will quote it. The Company's own C&LM forecast already puts expected heat pump load in Rate Year sales (CIEC-1(a)), which limits how much "beyond the forecast" there is. **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: RDM credit to non-residential classes per year from new heat pump adoption beyond the Company's forecast, Rate 1 vs Rate HP]**
:::

## CIEC-3

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 83, footnote 75, and page 101, lines 5-17.


a. Please explain why Mr. Velez did not propose a revenue-neutral seasonal design under which the winter reductions in Rate HP would be offset by higher summer distribution and transmission rates.
b. Would Mr. Velez object to a requirement that any revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP be recovered solely from the residential class? If so, explain why.
c. If any revenue reduction resulting from Rate HP were recovered solely from the residential class, please provide Mr. Velez’s estimate of the resulting increase in Rate 1 distribution and transmission charges, with supporting workpapers.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Because offsetting the winter reductions with higher summer rates for Rate HP customers would leave the overpayment in place.

   - The overpayment is the amount by which a heat pump customer's bill exceeds their pre-heat-pump bill plus incremental marginal cost.[^3a-define] A design that collects the same annual revenue from heat pump customers as Rate 1 collects the same overpayment, `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year on average, whatever its seasonal shape. It only moves the overpayment between seasons.[^3a-shifts]

     [^3a-define]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 24:8–10 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

     [^3a-shifts]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 101:7–10 (such a design "merely shifts the overpayment between seasons") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Footnote 75 does not propose such a design. It illustrates the Authority's authority to set a schedule-specific transmission rate without affecting wholesale obligations.[^3a-n75]

     [^3a-n75]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 83 n.75 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - A different design would offset the winter reductions with higher summer rates for _all_ residential customers on Rate 1. That is a choice about how to recover the existing-customer reduction within the residential class (part (b)), and summer is when marginal T&D costs occur.[^3a-summer] **[TK: JPV: do you want to offer this as acceptable? It changes Rate HP's summer rate too, since Rate HP's summer rates equal Rate 1's]**

     [^3a-summer]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 16:4–5 (distribution and transmission marginal costs "are concentrated entirely in the summer") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

b. No. Mr. Velez recommends it (CIEC-2(c)).

   - _New heat pump customers_ cause no reduction to recover.
   - _Existing heat pump customers_ cause the only reduction, which would be recovered from residential customers on Rate 1.

c. Estimates of the increase in Rate 1 rates, from recovering the existing-customer reduction from residential customers not on Rate HP.[^3c-method] Workpapers: `ciec_requests/ciec_request_3.qmd`, provided as CIEC-3 Attachment 1 **[TK: Alex Lee: export to Excel]**.

   [^3c-method]: The existing-customer reduction (CIEC-1(a)) divided by the Rate Year kWh of residential customers without heat pumps, `{python} num(c3.nonhp_kwh / 1e6)` million kWh in the model. The percentages compare the increase with Rate 1's proposed `{python} cents(FILED_TOTAL_DEL)` per kWh delivery rate.

   - The increase depends only on how many existing heat pump customers enroll; new heat pump customers add nothing to it.
   - Floor, `{python} num(c3.floor_existing)` existing heat pump customers (CIEC-1(b)): `{python} cents(c3.floor_per_kwh['dist'])` per kWh distribution and `{python} cents(c3.floor_per_kwh['tx'])` per kWh transmission, `{python} cents(c3.floor_per_kwh['total'])` in total, or `{python} pct(c3.floor_per_kwh['pct_of_td'], 1)` of Rate 1's delivery rate.
   - Ceiling, `{python} num(c3.ceiling_existing)` existing heat pump customers (CIEC-1(b)): `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['dist'])` distribution and `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['tx'])` transmission, `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['total'])` in total, or `{python} pct(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['pct_of_td'], 1)`.
   - **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: the non-heat-pump kWh above uses unscaled ResStock weights (`{python} num(c3.nonhp_customers)` non-heat-pump customers, from `{python} num(eia_cust['resstock_customers'])` ResStock households rather than the `{python} num(c1.rate_year_customers)` Rate Year customers), which overstates the per-kWh increase. Rescaled, the ceiling would be `{python} est("rate1_increase_ceiling_rescaled", cents)`. Rerun `ciec_request_3.qmd` with scaled weights before filing.]**

## CIEC-4

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 9, lines 1-7; page 17, lines 1-6; and page 18, lines 3-6.


a. Please confirm that, based on the figures in Velez Direct Testimony, the average fossil fuel-heated customer pays approximately $1,178 per year in distribution and transmission charges ($814 + $364) before installing a heat pump, while causing approximately $123 per year in marginal T&D costs.
b. Please explain why, under Mr. Velez’s methodology, the difference of approximately $1,055 per year between those two amounts is not also an “overcharge” or “overpayment.”
c. Please confirm that this difference represents the customer’s contribution to the recovery of the embedded costs of the Company’s existing transmission and distribution facilities. If Mr. Velez does not agree, explain what that difference represents.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Confirmed, with one clarification about what the `{python} dollar(pre_mc)` covers.

   - Before installing a heat pump, the average fossil fuel-heated customer pays `{python} dollar(pre_dist)` a year for distribution and `{python} dollar(pre_tx)` for transmission, `{python} dollar(pre_td)` in total, under proposed Rate 1. The distribution figure includes the riders billed with the Distribution Service Rate.[^4a-bill]

     [^4a-bill]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 9:3–6 (Oct. 21, 2026) (distribution "collected by the Distribution Service Rate and its associated riders (ESI, RDM, SBC, etc.) in Rate 1") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - That customer causes `{python} dollar(pre_mc)` a year in marginal T&D costs: `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_before)` upstream distribution and `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_before)` bulk transmission.[^4a-mc]

     [^4a-mc]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 18:3–6 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Clarification: the `{python} dollar(pre_mc)` counts only the capacity costs that usage can trigger. It leaves out the Company's marginal customer-related and local facilities costs, which are incurred when a customer connects and do not change with that customer's later usage. Together those come to `{python} dollar(mcos_connection_yr)` a year, against a customer charge of `{python} dollar(customer_charge_yr)` a year.[^4a-connection]

     [^4a-connection]: 12 × (`{python} dollar(MCOS_CUSTOMER_MO, 2)` customer-related + `{python} dollar(MCOS_LOCAL_FACILITIES_MO, 2)` local facilities) per month for Rate 1, from the Company's marginal cost of service study, against 12 × the proposed `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, 2)` monthly customer charge. [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 14 n.8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-3 at 243 (July 14, 2026) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

b. Measured against marginal cost alone, the customer does pay `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` a year more than the marginal T&D costs it causes. The testimony does not call that an overpayment, for three reasons.

   - The testimony defines the overpayment as a change: a customer's _incremental_ T&D charges after installing a heat pump, minus the _incremental_ marginal T&D cost the heat pump causes.[^4b-define] The `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` is a level, measured before any heat pump is installed, so it is outside that definition.

     [^4b-define]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 24:8–10 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Nearly every residential customer pays more than the marginal T&D costs it causes. The residential revenue requirement is set on embedded costs; the existing infrastructure must be paid for, but those are sunk costs, not costs caused by usage today.[^4b-sunk] Someone has to pay them.

     [^4b-sunk]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 13:23–14:2 (existing "infrastructure does need to be paid for, those are _sunk_ costs tied to old investments, not _marginal_ costs") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The testimony takes the Company's allocation of those embedded costs among residential customers as given, including each customer's pre-heat-pump share. It asks a narrower question: what should change when that customer installs a heat pump?
   - Under Rate 1, the answer is that the customer's payment toward embedded costs roughly doubles, from `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` to `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate1)` a year, while the heat pump adds only `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` a year in marginal T&D cost.[^4b-doubles] That increase is the `{python} dollar(overpay)` overpayment.

     [^4b-doubles]: After installing: (`{python} dollar(pre_td)` + `{python} dollar(inc_td)` in added T&D charges) − (`{python} dollar(pre_mc)` + `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` in added marginal T&D cost) = `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate1)`. [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 20:5–8, 23:3–5 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The customer's usage changed; the costs it causes barely did. The increase is a transfer to other residential customers, which is what the testimony calls a cross-subsidy.[^4b-cross]

     [^4b-cross]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 27:11–13 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Under Rate HP, the customer's payment toward embedded costs stays at about its pre-heat-pump level, `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate_hp)` a year on average (part (c) and CIEC-17).
   - Whether any customer's share of embedded costs should depend on kWh at all is a broader question about Rate 1's design. The testimony discusses one answer, a Rate 1 customer charge of `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, 2)` a month (CIEC-15), and does not recommend it.
   - **[COUNSEL / NRDC (mchhabra): JPV flagged this question as "the best retort to the incremental approach." Confirm the framing before filing.]**

c. Confirmed, with two qualifications.

   - Most of the difference is the customer's contribution to the embedded costs of existing distribution and transmission facilities.
   - Part of it pays for customer-related and local facilities costs: the customer charge covers `{python} dollar(customer_charge_yr)` of the `{python} dollar(mcos_connection_yr)` a year the Company's marginal cost study assigns to those costs (part (a)).
   - The transmission portion recovers the Company's wholesale transmission charges, which are themselves the embedded costs of the regional and local transmission network, passed to retail customers through the Transmission Adjustment Clause.[^4c-tac]

     [^4c-tac]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 83:5–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

:::

## CIEC-5

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 13, lines 18-23, and page 14, lines 1-11.


a. Mr. Velez states that existing T&D infrastructure “does need to be paid for.” Please explain how, under the cost causation framework in Velez Direct Testimony, the embedded costs of existing T&D infrastructure should be recovered and from whom.
b. If the incremental usage of a customer is priced at marginal T&D cost, as Mr. Velez proposes for heat pump load, please identify which customers would pay the embedded T&D costs that the incremental usage no longer contributes to.
c. Does Mr. Velez contend that the incremental load of commercial and industrial customers should likewise be priced at marginal T&D cost? Explain why or why not.
:::

::: {.response}
a. The same way they are recovered now. The testimony proposes no change to how the residential class's share of embedded T&D costs is set, and no change to any other class's share. Within the residential class, the recovery works as follows:

   - New heat pump customers: keep paying the embedded-cost contribution they paid before installing, about `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` a year for the average fossil fuel-heated home (CIEC-4), plus the incremental marginal cost their heat pump causes. Rate HP is calibrated to produce exactly that bill, on average.[^5a-calibrated] No embedded cost moves to anyone else.

     [^5a-calibrated]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 85:2–7 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Existing heat pump customers: pay the same Rate HP rates. Under Rate 1 they pay about `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year more toward embedded costs than they would without the heat pump (the overpayment); on Rate HP they stop paying that excess. For the average existing heat pump customer, the Rate HP bill is `{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)` a year lower than the Rate 1 bill (CIEC-1(a)).
   - Residential customers not on Rate HP: pay the same embedded-cost share as before, plus the existing customers' excess, which is recovered on Rate 1 when rates are set. That is the only change, and it unwinds the cross-subsidy the testimony describes. The increase is `{python} cents(c3.floor_per_kwh['total'])` to `{python} cents(c3.ceiling_per_kwh['total'])` per kWh (CIEC-3(c)).
   - Non-residential customers: no change. Their share of embedded costs is set by the class cost allocation, which Rate HP does not touch (CIEC-2(c) and CIEC-16(b)).

b. It depends on whether the incremental usage was already paying embedded costs when rates were set.

   - New heat pump customers: their heat pump usage was never part of the sales used to set Rate 1, so it was never counted on to contribute to embedded costs. Rate 1 already recovers the full residential revenue requirement without it. Pricing that usage near marginal cost takes nothing away from anyone. (See the caveat on the Company's C&LM forecast in CIEC-1(a) and CIEC-12(a).)
   - Existing heat pump customers: their heat pump usage is in the sales used to set rates. The embedded costs it stops contributing to are the shortfall in CIEC-1(a), recovered from residential customers on Rate 1 (part (a)).

c. No. The testimony takes no position on how commercial and industrial load should be priced.

   - The testimony addresses one problem: a group of residential customers whose usage rises structurally, mostly in winter, under volumetric rates designed for the class average. Whether incremental commercial or industrial load is overcharged would depend on those classes' rate designs and load shapes, which the testimony did not study.
   - The testimony does not propose to redesign rates for all customers. **[COUNSEL: JPV's sketch for this part reads "We are proposing a wholesale redesign"; the intended word is "not."]**
   - The Company itself has proposed pricing incremental large commercial and industrial load this way. Its proposed Economic Development Rate rider would discount the distribution charges on new or expanded load of Rate 57 (manufacturing) and Rate 58 customers, with demand generally above one megawatt.[^5c-edr] The discount is anchored to marginal cost, and it is limited to incremental load.[^5c-edr-floor]

     [^5c-edr]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 24:15–25:1 (July 14, 2026) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

     [^5c-edr-floor]: _Id._ at 28:5–6 (the discount is "anchored to the Company's marginal cost of service, which serves to support a minimum, marginal-cost-based charge"), 25:6–7 ("the EDR is limited to incremental (i.e., new or expanded) load only, and discounts shall not be available to existing load") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f].

   - The Company's rationale applies equally to new heat pump load.[^5c-edr-rationale]

     [^5c-edr-rationale]: _Id._ at 30:10–12 ("Incremental sales and revenue may contribute to lowering the rates for the recovery of costs through several reconciling mechanisms that would accrue to all customers, including EDR participants") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f].

   - The two proposals rest on the same principle: incremental load should pay at least the incremental cost it causes. They differ in one respect: the Economic Development Rate excludes existing load, while Rate HP enrolls existing heat pump customers, which is the source of the shortfall in CIEC-1(a).
   - **[UNVERIFIED IDEA]** CIEC may be testing for an undue-discrimination argument (marginal-cost pricing for one residential subgroup but not for commercial and industrial expansion load), or laying groundwork to support the Economic Development Rate, which its manufacturing members would be eligible for. Either way, the Company's own proposal answers the first.
:::

## CIEC-6

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 27, lines 3-8.


a. Please provide all analysis supporting the statement that the Company could eliminate the entire overpayment “without negatively affecting the bills of non-heat-pump customers.”
b. Please explain how that statement is consistent with recovery of the Company’s authorized revenue requirement between rate cases if revenue from heat pump customers is reduced.
c. Please provide Mr. Velez’s estimate of the bill impact of Rate HP on (i) residential customers who do not take service under Rate HP and (ii) non-residential customers, including those taking service under Rate 39 and Rate 57.
:::

::: {.response}
a. The statement concerns _new_ heat pump customers, who "would still be paying their full incremental cost of service."[^6a-new] The supporting analysis is the overpayment analysis in Sections III and IV of the testimony and Exhibit JPV-2, Sections 2–4:

   [^6a-new]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 27:6–8 (Oct. 21, 2026) ("customers newly installing heat pumps would still be paying their full incremental cost of service, still satisfying cost causation, without negatively affecting the bills of non-heat-pump customers") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - A fossil fuel-heated customer who installs a heat pump keeps paying their pre-heat-pump bill, which is what Rate 1 was set to collect from them, and on Rate HP adds the incremental marginal T&D cost of their new load.[^6a-calibrated] As a group, new heat pump customers' T&D payments rise by about `{python} dollar(c13.mean_bill_delta)` a year each (CIEC-13(b)).

     [^6a-calibrated]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Rates set in this case recover the revenue requirement from sales that do not include this new load (CIEC-12(a)). So other customers' rates need no increase to make up for anything new heat pump customers pay, and their bills are unaffected.
   - The Company's own standard is the same: a new customer's rate should cover the incremental cost of serving that customer, so that none of that customer's cost of service falls on other customers.[^6a-company-standard]

     [^6a-company-standard]: [CL&P Response to CLF-003(b)](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026), at 2 ("A Rate 6 customer pays to cover the incremental cost of serving that customer, such that no portion of that customer’s cost of service is redistributed to non-adopting customers.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026]; _see also_ [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 26:20–27:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The statement does not cover _existing_ heat pump customers, whose enrollment does lower revenue below what Rate 1 was set to collect. Their effect on other residential customers is in part (c).

b. The Company recovers its authorized revenue requirement either way; the question is who pays (CIEC-2(d)).

   - _New heat pump customers_ raise the Company's revenue between rate cases, as a group, so the reconciling mechanisms see an over-collection from them, not a shortfall.
   - _Existing heat pump customers_ lower it. Mr. Velez recommends building that reduction into Rate 1 in this rate case, and recovering any later difference from the residential class only (CIEC-2(c) and (d)). With those steps, non-residential customers' bills are unaffected.
   - Without them, an existing-customer shortfall between rate cases would flow through the Revenue Decoupling Mechanism, a flat rate per kWh across all classes, and about `{python} pct(nonres_kwh_share)` of it would fall on non-residential customers (CIEC-2(d)).[^6b-rdm]

     [^6b-rdm]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 22:21 (July 14, 2026) ("the rate will be set at a flat kWh rate across all rate classes") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

   - See the discussion in CIEC-2(d) on the RDM credit that non-residential customers receive today from heat pump load growth.

c. Estimates. Workpapers: `ciec_requests/ciec_request_6.qmd`, provided as CIEC-6 Attachment 1 **[TK: Alex Lee: export to Excel]**.

   - (i) Residential customers not on Rate HP:
     - _From new heat pump customers:_ no bill impact.
     - _From existing heat pump customers:_ an increase of `{python} cents(c6.floor_per_kwh)` to `{python} cents(c6.ceiling_per_kwh)` per kWh (CIEC-3(c)), or `{python} dollar(c6.floor_mean)` to `{python} dollar(c6.ceiling_mean)` a year for the average customer (median `{python} dollar(c6.floor_median)` to `{python} dollar(c6.ceiling_median)`), at the floor and ceiling enrollment estimates.
     - **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: same weight-scale issue as CIEC-3(c); rescaled, the ceiling average would be `{python} est("bill_impact_ceiling_rescaled")`. Rerun `ciec_request_6.qmd` before filing.]**
   - (ii) Non-residential customers, including Rates 39 and 57: `{python} dollar(c6.nonres_bill_impact)`, with the steps recommended in CIEC-2(c). Rate HP changes no non-residential rate and no class's share of the revenue requirement.
   - If the existing-customer reduction were instead left to the RDM (contrary to Mr. Velez's recommendation), non-residential customers would pay about `{python} pct(nonres_kwh_share)` of it: `{python} million(nonres_kwh_share * short_floor['dist'])` to `{python} million(nonres_kwh_share * short_ceiling['dist'])` a year of the distribution part, at a flat rate per kWh.[^6c-share] **[TK: Alex Lee: confirm the share from Exhibit CLP-RATES-2.12 and 2.4]**

     [^6c-share]: The non-residential share of Rate Year billed sales, as derived in CIEC-2(d), times the existing-customer distribution shortfall in CIEC-1(a).

## CIEC-7

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 15, lines 5-10; page 16, lines 1-5; and page 62, lines 11-14.


a. Please explain why Mr. Velez estimated marginal transmission cost using an avoided Pool Transmission Facility cost and the probability of the New England system peak, rather than the method by which regional and local network transmission costs are actually allocated to the Company.
b. Please describe Mr. Velez’s understanding of how ISO New England Inc. allocates regional network transmission service costs to the Company, including whether that allocation depends on the Company’s load at the time of the peak in each month.
c. Has Mr. Velez estimated the effect of heat pump adoption on the Company’s monthly peak loads during November through March, or on the transmission costs allocated to the Company? If so, provide the analysis. If not, explain why not.
d. Please explain how the 75% reduction in the winter Transmission Service Rate under Rate HP would affect the Company’s recovery of its transmission costs, and identify who would pay any resulting under-recovery.
:::

::: {.response}
> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** Read this before the bullets. You asked for both sides; here they are, then what the facts settle.
>
> _How it was chosen._ The transmission method mirrors the distribution method: an annual \$/kW cost spread over hours by probability of peak, as the Company did for distribution in OCC-733. It was not chosen after comparing it with the wholesale allocation. Part (a) says so plainly.
>
> _Side A: heat pumps cause transmission cost through the allocation formula._ CL&P pays Regional Network Service (RNS) and Local Network Service (LNS) on its load at each month's network peak, including November through March (part (b)). Every kW a heat pump adds at a winter monthly peak raises CL&P's RNS and LNS bill: about `{python} dollar(rnl_winter_cost_per_kw)` a year per kW present at all five winter monthly peaks, gross. The Company's own distribution planning guide counts "Monthly Regional and Local Network Services (RNS/LNS) Peak Reductions" as an avoided cost of batteries (CLF-SC-023 Attachment 1, in an older extract without page markers). From Connecticut's point of view this is real money.
>
> _Side B: the formula is not cost causation._ The regional pot is fixed by the transmission owners' revenue requirements; more Connecticut load shifts shares and lowers the RNS rate for everyone (2025 load growth lowered it by \$18/kW-year). AESC itself calls the share shift "a transfer within the region, rather than an avoided cost," and keeps it out of the \$69. LNS cannot leave Connecticut at all. FERC accepts monthly-peak (12CP) allocators partly because they "reduce yearly volatility," not as proof of causation, and the RAP manual rates 12CP's accuracy for cost causation "Low to medium." So a share shift is a cost to CL&P's customers, but not a cost the heat pump causes the region to incur.
>
> _A complication for both._ The \$69 comes from ISO-NE's 2050 study, whose investment is driven by future _winter_ peaks, but our method spreads it over summer-peaking 2022–2025 history. CIEC has not raised this yet.
>
> _What the facts settle._ (1) Under Rate 1, the representative home pays `{python} dollar(tx_inc_rev_rate1)` more in transmission after installing. Even on Side A's measure, that exceeds the added RNS and LNS cost unless the home adds more than about `{python} f"{breakeven_kw_rate1:.1f}"` kW at every winter monthly peak. Even if the full \$69 (inflated) were assigned to winter, the Rate 1 overpayment would remain (CIEC-9(c)). So the Rate 1 transmission overpayment survives either view, if per-home coincident load is moderate. (2) Rate HP is different: by design it collects only `{python} dollar(tx_inc_rev_rate_hp)` of incremental transmission revenue, which covers Side A's cost only below about `{python} f"{breakeven_kw_rate_hp:.2f}"` kW. If the Authority accepts Side A, the Rate HP winter TSR is too low. The Company's own floor for a winter transmission discount is "no less than the transmission service cost (i.e., the RNS plus LNS…)" (CL&P Response to CLF-SC-032 at 1). (3) The industrial firewall holds under both views: CL&P allocates transmission cost to classes by each class's monthly coincident peak (CLF-SC-032), so any added cost from residential winter load is allocated to the residential class, and the RNS and LNS rates per kW that commercial and industrial load pays go down slightly, not up.
>
> _Options._ (i) Keep the method and argue Side B, conceding the formula's effect on CL&P's bill; (ii) re-derive the Rate HP winter TSR to recover Side A's share-shift cost on incremental winter load (a higher winter TSR, still well below Rate 1); (iii) offer (ii) as a fallback if the Authority prefers Side A. Option (iii) fits a sharp intervenor best. **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: ResStock heat pump homes' added load at CL&P's (or Connecticut's) monthly peak hours, November–March, from the EIA/ISO-NE zone loads in `data/eia/hourly_loads/`; then the winter TSR that recovers RNS + LNS on that load]**

a. Mr. Velez estimated the marginal cost of transmission, the cost that additional load causes. The allocation method determines how existing costs are shared. He used a forward-looking cost, and spread it over hours the same way the Company spread distribution marginal cost, so that the two schedules would be consistent.

   - The Company computed no marginal cost of transmission.[^7a-no-mc]

     [^7a-no-mc]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-026](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 ("The Marginal cost of transmission was not computed for this rate design.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - Annual cost: the avoided Pool Transmission Facility cost of \$69/kW-year (2024 dollars) from the 2024 Avoided Energy Supply Components study, inflated to 2026 dollars. It is the cost of deferring regional transmission investment by one year through a one-year reduction in peak load.[^7a-aesc]

     [^7a-aesc]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 15:6–9 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; Synapse Energy Economics, _Avoided Energy Supply Components (AESC) in New England: 2024 Report_, at 17 (May 24, 2024) [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024] **[TK: AESC is not extracted, so this pinpoint is unverified; no public copy to link yet]**.

   - Hourly shape: the probability-of-peak method the Company's witness described for distribution in OCC-733, applied to New England system load for 2022–2025.[^7a-shape] The Company built that method on the sum of its distribution substation loads for the same years;[^7a-substation] Mr. Velez used regional load instead because pool transmission is planned to the regional peak **[TK: JPV: confirm this was the reason, or say it was chosen to mirror the distribution method]**. AESC directs that the value be applied to a measure's effect on the regional annual peak, whenever it occurs.[^7a-aesc-peak]

     [^7a-shape]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 15:9–16:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

     [^7a-substation]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-033](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 ("The sum of historical hourly Substation Loads from January 2022, to December 2025 across all the distribution substations provided by the Company were grouped by hour type…") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

     [^7a-aesc-peak]: AESC 2024 at 283–284 (the value applies "to a measure's impact on the regional annual system peak, regardless of when the peak occurs") [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024] **[TK: pinpoint unverified; AESC is not extracted]**.

   - Why not the wholesale allocation: RNS and LNS charges divide a fixed, already-incurred revenue requirement among network customers in proportion to their monthly peak loads (part (b)). A change in one customer's share is not a change in the cost of the transmission system. AESC excludes it from avoided transmission cost for that reason.[^7a-aesc-transfer]

     [^7a-aesc-transfer]: AESC 2024 at 285–286 (from a regional perspective, shifting existing RNS costs "would cause a transfer within the region, rather than an avoided cost") [@synapse_AvoidedEnergySupply_2024] **[TK: pinpoint unverified; AESC is not extracted]**.

   - Mr. Velez acknowledges that from CL&P's perspective a share shift does change what the Company pays. Its size relative to the transmission overpayment is discussed in part (c).
   - The investment behind the \$69 is driven by forecast winter peaks in 2050, while the hourly shape reflects today's summer-peaking system. As winter peaks approach, the hourly shape should be updated when Rate HP is recalibrated (CIEC-9(c)).

> **[COUNSEL]** The title printed inside the Figure 6 chart image reads "CT Eversource (PJM zone)"; the caption and text say CT Eversource and New England load (Velez Direct at 16, 16:1). CIEC may ask. Consider an errata to the figure.

b. Mr. Velez's understanding is that both regional and local network charges depend on the Company's load at the time of a monthly peak, in every month, including November through March:

   - RNS: each month, each network customer pays the RNS rate times its load at the hour of its Local Network's monthly peak, divided by 12. The RNS rate is the region's total Pool Transmission Facility revenue requirement divided by the 12-month average of the Local Networks' summed monthly peaks. CL&P is in the Northeast Utilities (now Eversource) Local Network.[^7b-rns]

     [^7b-rns]: ISO New England, [_Open Access Transmission Tariff, Section II_](https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/regulatory/tariff/sect_2/oatt/sect_ii.pdf), at Sections II.21.1–II.21.2, Schedule 9 and Attachment E ("the Local Network of the Northeast Utilities companies") (Sep. 1, 2026) [@isone_OpenAccessTransmission_2026] **[TK: the OATT is not extracted, so these pinpoints are unverified]**.

   - LNS: billed on load at the Eversource companies' monthly transmission system peak, with a Connecticut-specific rate equal to Connecticut's local revenue requirement divided by Connecticut load.[^7b-lns]

     [^7b-lns]: ISO New England, _Open Access Transmission Tariff_, Schedule 21-ES, at Sections 1.2 and 14.2 **[NOT INGESTED: inbox `isone_oatt_schedule_21_es.pdf`]**.

   - The Company describes the same structure: its transmission costs are set on monthly peak demand at rates based on the 12-month average peak,[^7b-031] and it allocates them to retail classes by each class's monthly coincident peak, recovered through an average annual rate per kWh for Rates 1 and 5.[^7b-032]

     [^7b-031]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-031](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (transmission costs are "determined on a monthly peak demand basis, at rates determined on a 12-month average peak demand") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

     [^7b-032]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-032](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (allocated "on the basis of the class's monthly coincident peak demand" and recovered through "an average annual transmission rate per kWh, for all hours under Residential Rate 1 and Rate 5") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - Three consequences. (1) More Connecticut load at a monthly peak raises CL&P's share of a fixed regional total and lowers the RNS rate per kW for everyone.[^7b-rns-rate] (2) LNS is recovered from Connecticut load whatever its timing; more load lowers the rate per kW. (3) Within CL&P, more residential load at winter monthly peaks raises the residential class's allocated share and lowers every other class's.

     [^7b-rns-rate]: The 2025 load change lowered the RNS rate by \$18.00/kW-year. Participating Transmission Owners Administrative Committee, RNS rate presentation, at 9 (July 16, 2026) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - Today, Connecticut's monthly network peaks are much lower in winter than in summer: for example, 6,500 MW in June 2025 against 4,702 MW in January 2026.[^7b-peaks]

     [^7b-peaks]: ISO New England, _Monthly Regional Network Load Cost Report_, at Table 7-1 (Apr. 2026) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

c. No. Mr. Velez has not estimated heat pump adoption's effect on the Company's November–March monthly peaks or on its allocated transmission costs, because the testimony measures marginal cost (part (a)), not shares of the regional charge. The Company's own forecasts do not yet include heat pump load at the winter peak.[^7c-forecast]

   [^7c-forecast]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-001(c)](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 2 ("Heat pump adjustments are not currently applied to our forecasted summer peak or winter peak demand (MW).") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

   - Scale: each kW a heat pump home adds at all five November–March monthly peaks would raise CL&P's RNS and LNS charges by about `{python} dollar(rnl_winter_cost_per_kw)` a year, gross, at current rates. Part of the RNS increase is offset by the lower RNS rate other networks pay.[^7c-scale]

     [^7c-scale]: (`{python} dollar(RNS_KW_YR, 2)`/kW-year RNS + `{python} dollar(LNS_CLP_KW_YR, 2)`/kW-year CL&P LNS) ÷ 12 × 5 months, plus `{python} dollar(RNL_OTHER_KW_MO, 3)`/kW-month of other network load charges × 5 months. RNS: Participating Transmission Owners Administrative Committee, RNS rate presentation (July 16, 2026) **[NOT INGESTED]**. LNS: Eversource, transmission rates web page **[NOT INGESTED]**. Other charges: ISO New England, _Monthly Regional Network Load Cost Report_, at Table 2-1 (Apr. 2026) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - At an assumed 2.5 kW per home that is `{python} est("rnl_share_shift")` a year **[EST]** **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: see the discussion block above]**.
   - Under Rate 1, the representative home pays `{python} dollar(tx_inc_rev_rate1)` a year more in transmission after installing a heat pump.[^7c-rate1-tx] That exceeds the gross share-shift cost unless the home adds more than about `{python} f"{breakeven_kw_rate1:.1f}"` kW at every winter monthly peak.

     [^7c-rate1-tx]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 12:7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - For comparison, ISO-NE forecasts Connecticut heat pumps adding 35 MW to the 2026 winter peak and 224 MW by 2030, against Connecticut monthly network peaks of about 3,800–4,800 MW in November–March.[^7c-isone]

     [^7c-isone]: ISO New England, [_Final 2026 Heat Pump Forecast_](https://pub.switch.box/isone_Final2026Heat_2026), at 24 (May 1, 2026) (Winter 50/50 Peak Demand by Load Zone, CT) [@isone_Final2026Heat_2026]; ISO New England, _Monthly Regional Network Load Cost Report_, at Table 7-1 (Apr. 2026) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - **[TK: decide on the discussion block's options; if (ii) or (iii), add the re-derived winter TSR here]**

d. Rate HP would lower the transmission revenue the Company collects from Rate HP customers in November through March. Its effect differs for new and existing heat pump customers:

   - _New heat pump customers:_ as a group, they keep paying their pre-heat-pump transmission bill plus the incremental transmission marginal cost (`{python} dollar(tx_inc_rev_rate_hp)` a year for the average home), so their transmission payments do not fall below what the Company collected from them before they installed. If their winter load raises CL&P's monthly peaks, CL&P's RNS and LNS charges rise (part (c)), and Rate HP does not collect that increase from them.
   - _Existing heat pump customers:_ their transmission payments fall by `{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)` a year each, for a total of `{python} million(short_floor['tx'])` to `{python} million(short_ceiling['tx'])` a year at the floor and ceiling enrollment estimates (CIEC-1(a)).
   - Recovery: the Company's transmission costs are fully reconciled through the Transmission Adjustment Clause, so the Company recovers them whatever Rate HP collects. The question is from which class.
   - Mr. Velez recommends that any difference be recovered from the residential class's transmission rate, as the Company does now: transmission cost is allocated to each class by its monthly coincident peak, and a winter discount would be made up from the same class's other rates.[^7d-within-class] Any added cost from residential winter load is allocated to the residential class by the same rule.

     [^7d-within-class]: CL&P Response to CLF-SC-032, at 1 (a winter discount for Rate 6 "would require an increase to the first block and non-winter second block rates, to achieve a design equivalent to meet total transmission revenue requirements for the class") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - Class rates are set from class allocations, but the TAC reconciliation is computed for the Company as a whole, and Mr. Velez has not found how the carried-forward balance is divided among classes (CIEC-2(d)). So Mr. Velez recommends that the Authority (1) build existing heat pump customers' Rate HP transmission revenue into this case's residential transmission rates, and (2) assign any later Rate HP difference to the residential class's transmission rate, not to the system-wide true-up (CIEC-2(c), step 3).
   - The Transmission Adjustment Clause adjusts on a fully reconciling basis.[^7d-tac]

     [^7d-tac]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-3 at 409 (July 14, 2026) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

:::

## CIEC-8

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 83, lines 3-16, and page 84, lines 1-12 and footnote 76.


a. Please explain Mr. Velez’s understanding of the basis for the difference between the Rate 5 and Rate 1 Transmission Service Rates, and state whether he contends that difference reflects marginal transmission cost.
b. Please explain Mr. Velez’s understanding of whether the winter transmission charges in the Massachusetts heat pump rates he describes were designed to recover a winter transmission revenue requirement or were instead set at an estimate of marginal transmission cost.
c. Please identify any jurisdiction of which Mr. Velez is aware that has set the retail transmission charges for a heat pump rate at an estimate of marginal transmission cost, and provide a copy of the relevant decision or tariff.
d. For each Massachusetts heat pump rate Mr. Velez describes, please explain his understanding of how any reduction in distribution or transmission revenue resulting from the rate is recovered, including whether any portion is recovered from non-residential customers.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Mr. Velez's understanding is that the difference reflects embedded-cost allocation, not marginal cost. He does not contend that it reflects marginal transmission cost.

   - The Company allocates its wholesale transmission expense to retail classes by each class's monthly coincident peak, and recovers each class's allocation through an average annual rate per kWh.[^8a-032]

     [^8a-032]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-032](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (allocated "on the basis of the class's monthly coincident peak demand" and recovered through "an average annual transmission rate per kWh, for all hours under Residential Rate 1 and Rate 5") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - Rate 5 is a separate class with its own revenue requirement; Rates 1 and 7 form another.[^8a-classes]

     [^8a-classes]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-006](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 ("in the filed allocated cost of service study, the cost to serve for Rate 5 Residential Space Heating customers has been provided, and the cost to serve for Rate 1 and Rate 7 includes all heating sources") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-035](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 ("Rate 7 is included in the cost allocation and overall revenue requirement along with Rate 1") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - So the 4.901¢ and 5.050¢ rates are each class's allocated share of the Company's embedded transmission expense divided by that class's kWh. Mr. Velez has not seen the calculation of the Rate 5 figure, which would be in the Company's Transmission Adjustment Clause filing **[RESEARCH: the TAC workbook (Exhibit G) computes one company-wide rate and takes the class rates from Docket 26-01-03, Order No. 3 Compliance Filing (Feb. 17, 2026), Exhibit 4, p. 3, and the April 22, 2026 Interim Decision; neither obtained]**.
   - The Company computed no marginal cost of transmission.[^8a-no-mc]

     [^8a-no-mc]: CL&P Response to CLF-SC-026, at 1 ("The Marginal cost of transmission was not computed for this rate design.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - The testimony cites the Rate 5 rate for one point only: the Authority already sets a different Transmission Service Rate for a specific residential schedule, so it can set a seasonal one for Rate HP.[^8a-rate5]

     [^8a-rate5]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 83:11–84:2 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

b. A winter transmission revenue requirement. The Massachusetts winter transmission charges recover the residential class's transmission revenue requirement over heat pump-adjusted winter sales; they were not set at an estimate of marginal transmission cost.

   - The DPU directed National Grid and Unitil to spread the winter transmission revenue requirement over adjusted winter sales.[^8b-directed]

     [^8b-directed]: D.P.U. 25-08-A, Order on Seasonal Heat Pump Rates, at 21 (June 1, 2026) (directing the companies to "recover the winter transmission revenue requirement over the adjusted winter sales") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026] **[TK: case caption; no public copy to link yet]**; _see also_ [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 84 n.76 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The DPU explained that "cost-based" meant revenue neutral, recovering embedded capital costs.[^8b-cost-based]

     [^8b-cost-based]: D.P.U. 25-08-A Order at 19 n.4 ("'cost-based' means that the winter transmission charges were structured to be revenue neutral, recovering the capital costs embedded in the transmission service revenue requirement through adjusted winter sales") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

   - NSTAR Electric's winter transmission price was calculated the same way, with the residential class's revenue target held constant.[^8b-nstar]

     [^8b-nstar]: D.P.U. 25-55, _Petition of NSTAR Electric Company, d/b/a Eversource Energy for Approval of Residential Seasonal Heat Pump Rates_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2555Order_2025), at 8 (July 29, 2025) (the winter transmission price "was then calculated to collect the winter transmission revenue requirement over the adjusted winter period sales") [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025]; [Direct Testimony of Richard D. Chin](https://pub.switch.box/chin_Docket2555Direct_2025) ("Chin Direct"), Exhibit ES-HP-1, D.P.U. 25-55, at 13:4 (Apr. 17, 2025) ("the revenue target for Rate R-1/R-2 … held constant") [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025].

   - The rationale for the seasonal split was cost causation in a summer-peaking system.[^8b-rationale]

     [^8b-rationale]: Chin Direct, Exhibit ES-HP-1, at 14:12–13 (transmission costs "are generally set in relation to system peak demand which typically happens in the summer") [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]; D.P.U. 25-08-A Order at 19 (base distribution and transmission costs are "well-suited to seasonal heat pump rate designs that reflect the timing and manner in which demand-related costs are incurred in a system that is currently summer peaking") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

   - The testimony cites Massachusetts for the precedent of a commission directing winter transmission reductions in heat pump rates, not for the method.[^8b-precedent] Rate HP's method differs: it lowers the winter rate until a heat pump customer's added transmission payment equals the added marginal cost, rather than spreading the class revenue requirement over assumed heat pump usage.

     [^8b-precedent]: Velez Direct at 84:3–12 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

c. Mr. Velez is not aware of any jurisdiction that has set a heat pump rate's retail transmission charge at an estimate of marginal transmission cost.

   - Rate HP does not do so either. Its winter Transmission Service Rate is set so that a new heat pump customer keeps paying their pre-heat-pump transmission bill, which contributes to embedded transmission costs, plus the incremental marginal cost.[^8c-calibrated] Only the increment is priced at marginal cost.

     [^8c-calibrated]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - A search on November 7, 2026 of heat pump and seasonal rates in Massachusetts, Maine, Rhode Island, New Hampshire, New York, Maryland, Connecticut, Minnesota, Colorado, Illinois, Michigan, Vermont, California, Québec and Ontario found none. The closest are:
     - Massachusetts: revenue-requirement based (part (b)).
     - Maine: Central Maine Power's A-Seasonal pilot collected all transmission and distribution kWh charges in May through October and none in November through April, a seasonal reallocation of the revenue requirement.[^8c-cmp] Maine's industrial customer group urged that heat pump rates put transmission and distribution costs on summer residential usage.[^8c-iecg]

       [^8c-cmp]: Me. P.U.C. Docket No. 2026-00248, Central Maine Power Company, [Request to Reinstate A-Seasonal (Heat Pump) Rate](https://pub.switch.box/cmp_Docket202600248Request_2026), at 1 (Aug. 25, 2026) ("All transmission and distribution kWh charges associated with the annual revenue requirement would be collected…") [@cmp_Docket202600248Request_2026].

       [^8c-iecg]: Me. P.U.C. Docket No. 2021-00325, [Revised Stipulation](https://pub.switch.box/cmp_Docket202100325Revised_2022), at 6 (Sept. 22, 2022) (heat pump rates should "allocate both transmission and distribution costs to summer residential electricity consumption") [@cmp_Docket202100325Revised_2022].

     - California: the Public Utilities Commission has encouraged utilities to propose an hourly marginal-cost-based transmission rate at FERC; none is in effect.[^8c-cpuc]

       [^8c-cpuc]: Cal. P.U.C. Decision D.25-08-049 **[NOT INGESTED: inbox `cpuc_decision_demand_flexibility_rate_guidelines_578182496.pdf`; pinpoint and date TK]**.

   - The Company did not compute marginal transmission cost for its own Rate 6.[^8c-no-mc]

     [^8c-no-mc]: CL&P Response to CLF-SC-026, at 1 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

d. Each Massachusetts rate is designed within the residential class; any actual shortfall from it flows into reconciling mechanisms, some of which allocate across all classes.

   - Design: each company sets the heat pump rates to recover the residential (R-1/R-2) class's target revenue on assumed heat pump usage.[^8d-design] The DPU found the rates revenue neutral to other customers.[^8d-neutral]

     [^8d-design]: Chin Direct, Exhibit ES-HP-1, at 13:4 [@chin_Docket2555Direct_2025]; D.P.U. 23-150, National Grid, [Exhibit HP-1, Residential Heat-Pump Rate Implementation Plan](https://pub.switch.box/meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024) ("National Grid Exhibit HP-1"), at 4 (Dec. 30, 2024) [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

     [^8d-neutral]: D.P.U. 25-08-A Order at 20 (the rates are "designed to be revenue neutral and will not increase costs to other customers beyond the cost to serve those customers") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

   - Actual shortfalls, base distribution: if heat pump usage is below the assumption, revenue falls short, and National Grid's tariff sends the shortfall to its Revenue Decoupling Mechanism.[^8d-rdm] National Grid's and Unitil's decoupling adjustments allocate a total-company shortfall across classes by fixed allocators, about 39% of it to non-residential classes.[^8d-allocators] Mr. Velez has not confirmed NSTAR Electric's allocation. **[TK: M.D.P.U. 1608 was superseded October 1, 2026 by M.D.P.U. 1635; confirm National Grid's current allocators before filing]**

     [^8d-rdm]: National Grid Exhibit HP-1 at 4 (the shortfall "will be included in the Company's Revenue Decoupling Mechanism") [@meco_Docket23150Exhibit_2024].

     [^8d-allocators]: National Grid, Revenue Decoupling Adjustment Provision, M.D.P.U. No. 1608, at 1, 3 **[NOT INGESTED]**; Unitil, Schedule RDAC, M.D.P.U. No. 500, at Sheets 5–6 **[NOT INGESTED]**.

   - Actual shortfalls, transmission: National Grid's transmission adjustment is calculated separately for each rate class **[TK: confirm from `meco_mdpu_1592_tsca_20250331.pdf` in the inbox]**.
   - The DPU expected decoupling to absorb shortfalls,[^8d-expected] and directed the companies to report heat pump customers' billed revenue against what they would have paid on the standard rate.[^8d-report]

     [^8d-expected]: D.P.U. 23-150, _Petition of Massachusetts Electric Company and Nantucket Electric Company, each d/b/a National Grid, pursuant to G.L. c. 164, § 94 and 220 CMR 5.00, for Approval of a General Increase in Base Distribution Rates for Electric Service, a Performance-Based Ratemaking Plan, and a Capital Recovery Mechanism_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket23150Order_2024), at 512 n.230 (Sept. 30, 2024) ("the Department expects there to be a reduced chance of significant revenue shortfalls … through the revenue decoupling mechanism") [@madpu_Docket23150Order_2024].

     [^8d-report]: D.P.U. 25-08-A Order at 1, 41 (directing the companies to report "the billed revenues recorded from heat pump customers in their annual revenue decoupling filings and to compare those revenues to the amounts that would have been billed if those customers had not enrolled in the heat pump rates") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026].

   - So Mr. Velez cannot say that no portion is recovered from non-residential customers in Massachusetts. For Connecticut he recommends that any Rate HP difference be reconciled within the residential class (CIEC-2(d) and CIEC-7(d)).
