## CIEC-9

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 7, lines 9-12; page 20, lines 9-12; page 22, lines 6-14; and page 59, footnote 63.


a. In footnote 63, Mr. Velez states that “a kWh consumed during a winter peak hour imposes far higher upstream distribution costs than a kWh consumed on a mild spring afternoon.” Please identify the winter peak hours to which this statement refers and explain how Rate HP’s winter distribution rate reflects them.
b. Has Mr. Velez analyzed the level of heat pump adoption at which the Company’s distribution system, or individual substations or feeders, would become winter peaking? If so, provide the analysis. If not, explain why not.
c. Please describe the specific process and timing Mr. Velez recommends for recalibrating Rate HP, and state whether he would support a requirement that Rate HP be recalibrated, or automatically expire, if winter loads begin to drive distribution capacity investment.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Footnote 63 does not refer to specific winter peak hours on the Company's system. It contrasts a static marginal cost, applied equally to every kWh, with a dynamic one that varies by hour, and uses a winter peak hour as a generic example.[^9a-n63] On the Company's system today, there are no winter peak hours, and Rate HP's winter rate reflects that.

   [^9a-n63]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 59 n.63 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The hourly upstream distribution marginal costs come from the Company's own probability-of-peak allocation.[^9a-pop]

     [^9a-pop]: CL&P Response to OCC-863 **[NOT INGESTED]**; [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 14:14–21 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - In that allocation, `{python} pct(m.pct_dist_mc_peak_hours_summer)` of the hours carrying a meaningful marginal distribution cost fall in April through October.[^9a-summer]

     [^9a-summer]: Velez Direct at 16:4–5 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - For the average fossil fuel-heated home, the marginal T&D cost of all November-through-March usage is `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_seasonal_mc_delivery_winter_before, 2)` a year before installing a heat pump and `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_seasonal_mc_delivery_winter_after, 2)` after.[^9a-winter-mc]

     [^9a-winter-mc]: Velez Direct at 20:5–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Rate HP's winter rate is set so the average customer's T&D bill equals the pre-heat-pump bill plus incremental marginal cost.[^9a-calibrated] Because winter usage carries almost no marginal cost, the winter rate falls until the added winter kWh add almost nothing to the bill.

     [^9a-calibrated]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The winter rate is not zero because it still collects the customer's pre-heat-pump winter contribution to embedded costs (CIEC-17).
   - If winter peak hours appear in a future probability-of-peak analysis, recalibration would raise the winter rate (part (c)).

b. No. The Company's distribution system as a whole is not close to becoming winter peaking; individual feeders and substations would become winter peaking first, and that would require feeder- and substation-level data that has not yet been produced.

   - System: the Company says the system remains summer peaking, and it does not use a heat pump forecast for substation capacity projects.[^9b-summer-peaking]

     [^9b-summer-peaking]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-020](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 ("The Company currently does not use a heat pump forecast to inform its substation capacity projects as the system remains summer peaking.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

   - The Company has no completed winter peak forecast. Its unreleased forecast reaches only a preliminary substation level, and feeder- and transformer-level forecasts are not expected until 2028.[^9b-021] Its heat pump forecasts have not been released.[^9b-022]

     [^9b-021]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-021](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c), at 1 ("Under the current unreleased forecast only a preliminary substation level could be created. Feeder and transformer level forecasts will be available for the 2028 forecast.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c].

     [^9b-022]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-022](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c), at 2 ("Currently, the Company's heat pump forecasts have not been released.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c].

   - What we requested: for every feeder and substation transformer, summer and winter ratings, summer and winter peaks with their dates and hours, and forecast peaks (CLF-SC-012 to CLF-SC-019).
   - What the Company said: the data is Critical Energy Infrastructure Information, and it will produce it once CLF-SC signs a non-disclosure agreement and the Company finishes new cybersecurity document controls.[^9b-ndas] **[COUNSEL: current NDA status; date signed or expected]**

     [^9b-ndas]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-012](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1–2 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; CL&P Response to CLF-SC-013, at 2 (production will follow "once an executed NDA is obtained from CLF-SC") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; _see also_ CL&P Responses to CLF-SC-014 to CLF-SC-019 (same).

   - What the data would show: each feeder's and substation's winter headroom, and the number of additional heat pump customers at which its winter peak would exceed its rating.
   - What we have now: annual peak loading for 918 feeders, without the season of the peak. The median feeder peaks at 49% of its rating, and 2 exceed their rating.[^9b-feeders]

     [^9b-feeders]: Velez Direct at 21:5–8, 22:1–3 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - We will supplement this response within **[COUNSEL: number]** days of receiving the data.

c. Recalibrate Rate HP in each rate case, using an updated marginal cost study whose probability-of-peak analysis includes heat pump load.[^9c-recalibrate] Mr. Velez would support a requirement to recalibrate; he would not support automatic expiry.

   [^9c-recalibrate]: Velez Direct at 7:9–12 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Each recalibration repeats the calculation in the testimony: find the winter rates at which the average new heat pump customer's T&D bill equals the pre-heat-pump bill plus incremental marginal cost.[^9c-calibrated]

     [^9c-calibrated]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The probability-of-peak analysis should use substation and feeder loads that reflect actual heat pump adoption. The Authority could require it more often than each rate case if adoption accelerates.
   - Recalibration already does what an expiry trigger would try to do. As feeders and substations become winter peaking, the analysis moves peak hours and marginal cost into winter, heat pump customers' incremental marginal cost rises, and the winter rate rises with it.
   - Rate HP would no longer be needed only when heat pump customers' incremental marginal cost reached their incremental Rate 1 charges: about `{python} num(td_to_mc_multiple)` times today's `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` a year.[^9c-multiple]

     [^9c-multiple]: The representative home's incremental Rate 1 T&D charges, `{python} dollar(inc_td)`, divided by its incremental marginal cost, `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)`. Velez Direct at 23:3–5 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Rough scale: if all marginal T&D capacity cost were assigned to winter peak hours instead of summer, the representative home's incremental marginal cost would be about `{python} est("winter_peak_mc")` a year, and its overpayment under Rate 1 would still be about `{python} dollar(overpay - (EST["winter_peak_mc"][0] - inc_mc))` [EST]. **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: winter probability-of-peak "reach" run (Google Doc comment 18)]**
   - An expiry triggered by "winter loads begin[ning] to drive distribution capacity investment" would end the rate when the first feeders turned winter peaking, while heat pump customers as a group were still overpaying by most of the `{python} dollar(overpay)`.
   - Mr. Velez would support a reporting requirement, for example the Company reporting heat pump customers' billed revenue against the Rate 1 revenue they would have paid, as Massachusetts requires in decoupling filings (CIEC-8(d)).
:::

## CIEC-10

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 10, footnote 4; page 19, lines 4-8; and page 20, lines 5-8.


a. Footnote 4 states that the heat pumps modeled include “electric resistance backup.” Please provide the modeled hourly electric resistance backup load for the average fossil fuel-heated home after heat pump installation, and identify the hours of highest heat pump and backup load in the modeled year.
b. Please explain how the incremental marginal T&D cost of $10 per year reflects heat pump and electric resistance backup load during extreme cold weather conditions more severe than those in the modeled weather year.
c. Please provide the hourly calculation underlying the $10 per year estimate in Excel format with formulas intact.
:::

::: {.response}
a. The modeled heat pumps are ResStock's cold-climate air-source heat pumps with electric resistance backup.[^10a-n4] The backup load was not reported separately in the testimony's analysis; it will be provided as CIEC-10 Attachment 1 **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: weighted hourly backup kWh and total heat pump kWh for the fossil fuel-heated sample after the upgrade, from ResStock's end-use columns; the hours of highest total and backup load. Low priority (Google Doc comment 19)]**.

   [^10a-n4]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 10 n.4 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Rough scale until then: `{python} est("backup_kwh", num)` kWh a year of backup, out of `{python} num(r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_after - r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` kWh of incremental usage.
   - Whatever its size, the backup load falls in November through March, when the hours carry almost no marginal T&D cost under the Company's probability-of-peak allocation (CIEC-9(a)). It is included in the `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)`.

b. The `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` reflects heat pump and backup load in the modeled weather year, priced at the hourly marginal costs from the Company's probability-of-peak analysis. It does not model a winter colder than that.

   - Load: ResStock's AMY2018 release, which simulates each home in the actual weather of 2018 **[RESEARCH: how severe winter 2017–18 was in Connecticut relative to the Company's planning conditions; check NOAA heating degree days and the early-January 2018 cold snap]**.
   - Distribution marginal cost: the Company's probability-of-peak analysis, built from hourly substation loads for January 2022 through December 2025 and simulated 500 times with kernel density estimation.[^10b-pop] Winter hours in that history, cold ones included, received almost no probability of being the peak.

     [^10b-pop]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-033](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1–2 (reprinting the Company's response to OCC-733; "the model simulated hourly load distributions 500 times using a truncated version of Gaussian Kernel density estimation (KDE)" at 2) [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

   - Transmission marginal cost: the same method applied to ISO New England system load for 2022 through 2025.[^10b-tx]

     [^10b-tx]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 15:6–16:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The Company plans capacity for an extreme summer: only its 90/10 peak forecast informs capacity projects, and its peak model uses summer weather variables.[^10b-9010]

     [^10b-9010]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-022](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c), at 4 ("Only the 90/10 scenario is used to inform the Company's capacity projects."), 2 ("two different weather variables in forecasting summer peak demand, a three-day weighted temperature-humidity index and cooling degree days") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026c].

   - A colder winter would raise heat pump and backup load in winter hours. That would add marginal cost only where winter load approached a feeder's or substation's rating. The median feeder peaks at 49% of its rating today.[^10b-feeders]

     [^10b-feeders]: Velez Direct at 21:7–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]. The seasonal data that would show winter headroom is withheld pending an NDA (CIEC-9(b)).

   - Concession: the `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` is an expected value under the Company's planning data, not a design-day estimate. For the overpayment to disappear, incremental marginal cost would have to be about `{python} num(td_to_mc_multiple)` times larger (CIEC-9(c)).

c. Provided as CIEC-10 Attachment 1: the representative home's hourly load before and after the heat pump, the hourly distribution and transmission marginal costs, and their product summed to `{python} dollar(inc_mc, 2)` **[TK: Alex Lee: confirm the representative-home workbook (Exhibit JPV-3) holds these columns and sums to the testimony figure (Google Doc comment 22)]**.

## CIEC-11

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 8, lines 1-2 and footnote 1, and page 10, lines 4-7.


a. Please describe any steps Mr. Velez took to validate or calibrate the ResStock simulated load profiles against the Company’s actual residential loads, and provide the results.
b. Please provide a comparison of the simulated average annual and monthly usage of the modeled homes before heat pump installation with the Company’s actual average residential usage.
c. Please provide all CAIRO model input and output files used in Velez Direct Testimony that have not already been provided in Exhibits JPV-3 and JPV-4 or in response to CIEC-1.
:::

::: {.response}
a. ResStock's simulated loads were compared against two benchmarks, and the number of modeled households was calibrated to the Company's filed customer count. The loads themselves were not adjusted.

   - Calibration: ResStock assigns `{python} num(eia_cust['resstock_customers'])` households to the Company's territory. The weights were scaled to the `{python} num(c1.rate_year_customers)` residential customers the Company filed for the Rate Year.[^11a-customers] The scaling is uniform, so it changes totals, not per-customer bills or shares.

     [^11a-customers]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-2.10 (July 14, 2026) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g] **[TK: no public copy to link yet; sheet pinpoint]**; Exhibit JPV-2, Section 1.

   - Check 1, EIA-861 (2018, matching ResStock's weather year): the ResStock average Eversource home uses `{python} num(resstock_kwh_per_customer)` kWh a year, against `{python} num(eia_kwh_per_customer)` kWh per residential customer in EIA-861, `{python} pct(eia_kwh['kwh_pct_diff'] / 100, 1)`.[^11a-eia]

     [^11a-eia]: U.S. Energy Information Administration, [_Form EIA-861 Annual Electric Power Industry Report_](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861/), 2018 data, The Connecticut Light and Power Company, residential sales divided by residential customers [@eia_EIA861AnnualElectric_2026].

   - Check 2, the Company's 2025 class-average hourly loads for Rates 1 and 5 **[TK: Alex Lee: which discovery response provided this workbook?]**, compared hour by hour with the weighted-average ResStock home of the matching heating type (part (b)).
   - The Company could not provide loads by heating type: it does not track customers' heating source and, apart from small samples, has no interval meters.[^11a-no-data] So no check of heat pump homes' loads against measured heat pump loads was possible.

     [^11a-no-data]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-003](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 ("the Company does not track the heating sources of its customers") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; CL&P Response to CLF-SC-008, at 1 ("The Company does not employ AMI meters and does not have the data requested.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

b. Comparison of modeled and actual average usage before heat pump installation. Monthly figures are in CIEC-11 Attachment 1 **[TK: Alex Lee: export the two monthly tables from `notebooks/eversource_hourly_class_loads.qmd` to Excel]**.

   - Company average, all residential customers: `{python} num(rate_year_kwh_per_customer)` kWh a year in the Rate Year forecast.[^11b-rate-year] ResStock average, all Eversource homes: `{python} num(resstock_kwh_per_customer)` kWh in 2018 weather.

     [^11b-rate-year]: `{python} num(CLASS_BILLED_MWH)` MWh of Rate Year billed residential sales divided by `{python} num(fc.class_customers)` customers. Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-2 [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026g] **[TK: sheet pinpoints]**.

   - Fossil fuel-heated homes against Rate 1: the Company's average Rate 1 customer used `{python} num(c11_r1['Annual']['company_kwh'])` kWh in 2025; the ResStock homes heated with gas, delivered fuels or other fuels use `{python} num(c11_r1['Annual']['resstock_kwh'])` kWh. The Company figure is `{python} pct(c11_r1['Annual']['pct_diff'], 1)` higher.
   - By month, the Rate 1 gap is largest in July (`{python} pct(c11_r1['Jul']['pct_diff'])`), June (`{python} pct(c11_r1['Jun']['pct_diff'])`) and December through February (`{python} pct(min(c11_r1[mo]['pct_diff'] for mo in ['Dec', 'Jan', 'Feb']))` to `{python} pct(max(c11_r1[mo]['pct_diff'] for mo in ['Dec', 'Jan', 'Feb']))`), and within ±`{python} pct(max(abs(c11_r1[mo]['pct_diff']) for mo in ['Mar', 'Apr', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct']))` in March, April and August through October.
   - Electric-heated homes against Rate 5 (Residential Electric Heating Service): the Company's average Rate 5 customer used `{python} num(c11_r5['Annual']['company_kwh'])` kWh in 2025; the ResStock homes heated with electric resistance or heat pumps use `{python} num(c11_r5['Annual']['resstock_kwh'])` kWh, so the Company figure is `{python} pct(-c11_r5['Annual']['pct_diff'], 1)` lower. In November through March it is `{python} pct(-c11_r5_winter_pct)` lower.
   - Caveats on both comparisons: the Company's figures are 2025 weather and ResStock's are 2018; Rate 1 also serves some electric-heated and heat pump customers, and Rate 5 does not serve every electric-heated home.

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** The Rate 5 gap is the one CIEC could use. If ResStock overstates electric heating load by 20–30% in winter, it may overstate the incremental kWh after a heat pump retrofit, and the overpayment scales roughly with incremental kWh (each one is billed at about 16¢ against almost no marginal cost). Two things may cut the other way: Rate 5 customers may be a different population from ResStock's electric-heated homes (**[UNVERIFIED IDEA]** for example, more resistance-heated apartments on Rate 5, and some electric-heated houses on Rate 1), and 2025 may have been milder than 2018. Before filing, it is worth (1) weather-normalizing the comparison with heating degree days for 2018 and 2025, and (2) checking whether the Rate 1 gap (ResStock lower) and the Rate 5 gap (ResStock higher) partly offset in the pre/post comparison. The Rate 1 gap barely matters for the overpayment, which is a difference. **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: weather-normalized version of the Rate 5 comparison]**

## CIEC-12

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 7, lines 3-8; page 93, lines 7-12; and page 96, lines 1-12.


a. Does Mr. Velez agree that the load of existing heat pump customers is already on the Company’s system and reflected in the sales used to set the Company’s rates in this proceeding? If not, explain why not.
b. Please identify any new load, or any reduction in the Company’s costs, that would result from enrolling existing heat pump customers in Rate HP.
c. Please provide Mr. Velez’s estimate of the annual reduction in distribution and transmission revenue attributable solely to the automatic enrollment of existing heat pump customers.
d. Please explain how the “pre-heat-pump T&D bill” referenced at page 85, lines 5-7 would be determined for an existing heat pump customer.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Yes. Existing heat pump customers' load is on the system and in the sales used to set rates in this proceeding. Enrolling them in Rate HP lowers revenue below what Rate 1 was set to collect from them. This is why, throughout these responses:

   - _New heat pump customers_ (installing after Rate HP takes effect) create no shortfall: their heat pump load is not in the sales used to set rates, and as a group they pay more after installing than before.
   - _Existing heat pump customers_ (installed before) create the only shortfall: their heat pump load is in those sales, and Rate HP collects less from them than Rate 1.
   - One refinement: the Company's Rate Year sales forecast already includes heat pumps it expects to install through its Conservation and Load Management programs.[^12a-forecast] For this purpose, load forecast in this way behaves like existing customers' load: the precise dividing line is heat pump load already in the sales used to set rates versus load that is not **[TK: JPV: settle with the CIEC-1(a) discussion]**.

     [^12a-forecast]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-001](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 (heat pump adjustments to the sales forecast "are based on the CT C&LM programs forecast") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; CL&P Response to CLF-SC-002, at 1 ("Heat pump or electrification adjustments are made to the Company’s sales forecast for the heating months (October-April) based off the 2025-2027 Energy Efficiency Plan.") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

   - Rate HP charges new and existing heat pump customers the same rates, because they receive the same service at the same marginal cost.[^12a-same-service] What differs is only the effect on the Company's revenue of moving each group to that rate.

     [^12a-same-service]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 58:8–10 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

b. None. Enrolling existing heat pump customers adds no load and reduces no cost. It lowers what they pay, which the testimony shows is more than the costs they cause.[^12b-overcharged]

   [^12b-overcharged]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 5:14–16 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The purpose is to stop an existing overcharge: on Rate 1 they pay about `{python} dollar(overpay)` a year more than their pre-heat-pump bill plus incremental marginal cost, and that excess lowers other residential customers' rates.[^12b-existing]

     [^12b-existing]: Velez Direct at 96:3–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The Company's Rate 6 makes the opposite choice: by limiting eligibility by installation date it avoids the revenue effect but leaves existing heat pump customers overpaying.[^12b-rate6]

     [^12b-rate6]: _Id._ [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

c. `{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)` a year per existing heat pump customer (`{python} dollar(c1.dec_dist, 2)` distribution, `{python} dollar(c1.dec_tx, 2)` transmission), or `{python} million(short_floor['total'])` to `{python} million(short_ceiling['total'])` a year at the floor (`{python} num(floor_existing)`) and ceiling (`{python} num(ceiling_existing)`) enrollment estimates (CIEC-1(a)).

   - Of that, distribution: `{python} million(short_floor['dist'])` to `{python} million(short_ceiling['dist'])`; transmission: `{python} million(short_floor['tx'])` to `{python} million(short_ceiling['tx'])`.
   - The per-customer figure rests on the `{python} num(c1.n_bldg)` ResStock buildings that already have heat pumps **[TK: Alex Lee: confirm the sample is adequate, or bootstrap a range (Google Doc comment on CIEC-1)]**.
   - None of this is attributable to new heat pump customers.

d. Rate HP does not need a customer-specific pre-heat-pump bill. The rate is set once, from the average fossil fuel-heated home's bill before and after installation,[^12d-calibrated] and the same rate then applies to every enrolled customer, new or existing.

   [^12d-calibrated]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026]; Exhibit JPV-2, Section 5.

   - The phrase at 85:5–7 describes how the rate is calibrated, not a calculation made for each customer's bill.
   - For an existing heat pump customer, the relevant comparison is what a fossil fuel-heated home like theirs would have paid before installing. Their own history may not show it (they may have installed years ago, or moved into a home with a heat pump), and Rate HP does not use it.
:::

## CIEC-13

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 7, lines 3-6, and page 93, lines 1-6.


a. Please describe how Mr. Velez proposes that the Company verify that a customer enrolled in Rate HP has installed a heat pump and uses it as the customer’s primary source of space heating.
b. Would customers that use a heat pump only as a supplemental heating source, while retaining a fossil fuel heating system, be eligible for Rate HP? Explain.
c. Would customers that heat with electric resistance, or that install ground-source heat pumps, be eligible for Rate HP? Explain.
d. Under Rate HP, would winter usage from end uses other than space heating, such as electric vehicle charging, receive the reduced winter rates? If so, please estimate the associated revenue reduction and explain why that result is consistent with cost causation.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Mr. Velez proposes verifying that a heat pump is installed and used for heating. He does not propose a test of whether it is the primary heating source; Rate HP is for customers who use a heat pump for heating.[^13a-who]

   [^13a-who]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 6:13–14 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - New installations through Energize CT or the New England Heat Pump Accelerator: the program's incentive records identify the customer, who is auto-enrolled at installation.[^13a-new]

     [^13a-new]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 93:1–4 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Self-funded installations: an attestation and certification form submitted by the installer or the customer.[^13a-self]

     [^13a-self]: Velez Direct at 93:4–6 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Existing heat pump customers: auto-enrollment from past incentive records, and attestation for the rest.[^13a-existing]

     [^13a-existing]: Velez Direct at 93:7–12, 96:9–11 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The Company cannot identify heat pump customers from its own data: it does not track heating source and has no interval meters.[^13a-no-data]

     [^13a-no-data]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-003](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; CL&P Response to CLF-SC-008, at 1 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b].

   - Mr. Velez would support documentary proof with audit rights for customers outside the incentive programs, as Eversource's Massachusetts affiliate requires, with the right to audit and to remove customers whose documents cannot be confirmed.[^13a-nstar] National Grid's Massachusetts tariff is similar; Unitil accepts a customer's affirmation of ownership.[^13a-ng-unitil]

     [^13a-nstar]: D.P.U. 25-55, NSTAR Electric Company d/b/a Eversource Energy, [Exhibit ES-HP-5, Residential Heat Pump Rate Implementation Plan](https://pub.switch.box/nstarelectric_Docket2555Residential_2025), at 5 (Apr. 17, 2025) (proof may be "photos of equipment serial numbers; proof of payment or receipt of equipment purchase; or invoice or receipt from contractor installation") [@nstarelectric_Docket2555Residential_2025].

     [^13a-ng-unitil]: National Grid, Residential Heat Pump Rate Provision, M.D.P.U. No. 1634, at 2 **[NOT INGESTED: inbox `meco_mdpu_1634_r1_provision_2026.pdf`]**; Unitil, Residential Heat Pump Rate Schedule, M.D.P.U. No. 496, at Sheet 3 **[NOT INGESTED: inbox `unitil_fge_hp_res_schedule_mdpu_496.pdf`]**.

> **[COUNSEL]** Velez Direct at 94:10–16 (1) attributes Massachusetts's approval of the heat pump rates to D.P.U. 25-08; they were approved in D.P.U. 23-80 (Unitil), 23-150 (National Grid) and 25-55 (NSTAR Electric), and 25-08 is the later statewide inquiry; and (2) says Massachusetts uses "an attestation process" for prior installations, which describes Unitil only; Eversource and National Grid require documents. Consider an errata.

b. Yes. Rate HP is available to any customer using a heat pump for heating, including one that supplements a fossil fuel system.

   - Massachusetts does the same: all three rates cover heat pumps that supplement another heat source or heat part of the home,[^13b-ma-def] and the DPU has repeatedly declined the Attorney General's request to limit eligibility to heat pumps sized for the whole home.[^13b-ma-ag]

     [^13b-ma-def]: D.P.U. 25-55, _Petition of NSTAR Electric Company, d/b/a Eversource Energy for Approval of Residential Seasonal Heat Pump Rates_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2555Order_2025), at 5 n.8 (July 29, 2025) (quoting the NSTAR Electric tariff: devices "used to heat or supplement another heat source for their home or part of their home") [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025].

     [^13b-ma-ag]: D.P.U. 25-55 Order at 22 ("Therefore, we decline to accept the Attorney General’s recommendation at this time.") [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025]; D.P.U. 23-80/D.P.U. 23-81, _Petition of Fitchburg Gas and Electric Light Company d/b/a Unitil (Electric Division), pursuant to G.L. c. 164, § 94 and 220 CMR 5.00, for Approval of a General Increase in Base Distribution Rates for Electric Service and a Performance-Based Ratemaking Plan_, [Order](https://pub.switch.box/madpu_Docket2380Order_2024), at 407 (June 28, 2024) ("we decline to limit the rate offering only to customers with heat-pump capacity sized to heat their entire home, as suggested by the Attorney General") [@madpu_Docket2380Order_2024].

   - Rate HP is calibrated on the average fossil fuel-heated home converting to a heat pump with electric backup. Individual customers' bills move around that average: across the modeled homes, the annual T&D bill rises on average by `{python} dollar(c13.mean_bill_delta, 2)`, close to their `{python} dollar(c13.mean_delta_mc, 2)` average incremental marginal cost, but `{python} pct(c13.pct_bill_decrease)` of homes would see it fall after installing, and `{python} pct(c13.pct_bill_increase_100)` would see it rise by more than \$100.
   - A customer whose winter usage rises less than average (for example, a heat pump heating part of the home) would pay less on Rate HP than before installing. That is a revenue reduction attributable to that new customer, and it is offset, within the group, by customers whose usage rises more than average.
   - New heat pump customers as a group create no shortfall only if their mix of usage increases resembles the calibration population. The Company's recalibration in each rate case and the reporting proposed in CIEC-9(c) would show whether it does.

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** This part is where the "new customers create no shortfall" line is most exposed, and CIEC will see it. Facts: under Rate HP, `{python} pct(c13.pct_bill_decrease)` of modeled new adopters pay less T&D than before installing (`{python} pct(c13.pct_bill_decrease_100)` by more than \$100), and the group pays `{python} dollar(c13.mean_bill_delta)` more each. Why: the winter rate is about one-quarter of Rate 1, so a home whose November–March usage rises less than `{python} f"{breakeven_winter_ratio:.1f}"`-fold pays less in winter than before, and only April–October load at full rates makes it up (CIEC-14(a)). The group claim holds by construction; the individual claim does not, and Velez Direct at 95:14–16 makes exactly this argument against a rate open to all customers. Options: (1) say it as above, with "as a group" everywhere (already added to the formulation in CIEC-1(a)); (2) propose that supplemental heat pumps qualify only through the incentive programs, which record whether the system is full or partial displacement (the Company counts "approximately 4,400 customers who have received heat pump rebates that indicate full displacement of other heat sources," CL&P Response to CLF-SC-003, at 1); (3) calibrate Rate HP on the expected adopter mix rather than full conversions. Massachusetts accepted partial-home customers and relied on decoupling to catch shortfalls (D.P.U. 23-150 Order at 512 n.230), which there spreads them across classes (CIEC-8(d)). Option 2 or 3 would be stronger for this intervenor. **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: the same share for natural gas vs. delivered fuel homes is already computed (`notebooks/overpayment.qmd`); if option 3, a partial-displacement scenario]**

c. Electric resistance: no, unless the customer also installs a heat pump; ground-source heat pumps: yes.

   - Electric resistance heat does not qualify on its own. Electric resistance customers who install a heat pump qualify, whatever heating system they had before.[^13c-resistance]

     [^13c-resistance]: Velez Direct at 81:15–16 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Rate HP was calibrated on fossil fuel-heated homes converting to heat pumps. An electric resistance home's usage falls when it installs a heat pump, so it does not cause the overpayment Rate HP corrects.
   - Ground-source heat pumps qualify. They lower winter usage relative to air-source heat pumps, so a customer converting from fossil fuel with one would add less winter load (part (b) applies). Massachusetts interprets its definition to include them.[^13c-gshp]

     [^13c-gshp]: D.P.U. 25-55 Order at 5 n.8 [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025].

   - Rate 5 (Residential Electric Heating Service) remains available to electric resistance customers; Rate HP does not replace it. Massachusetts likewise kept its electric space heating rates open alongside its heat pump rates.[^13c-r3]

     [^13c-r3]: D.P.U. 25-55 Order at 22–23 ("the Department rejects the Company’s proposal to close Rate R-3 and Rate R-4 to new customers at this time") [@madpu_Docket2555Order_2025].

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** The testimony makes electric resistance customers who install heat pumps eligible (81:15–16), but the new/existing split assumes new customers are fossil conversions. A new customer converting from electric resistance (many on Rate 5) would pay far less on Rate HP than before: winter usage falls and the winter rate falls about 76%. That is a revenue reduction from a _new_ customer, which the CIEC-1 figures do not include and the "new customers create no shortfall" line does not cover. Options: (1) limit new enrollment to customers converting from fossil fuel heat (incentive records show the prior system); (2) keep them eligible and count them with existing customers in the shortfall estimate; (3) leave Rate 5 as their rate and make Rate 5 customers ineligible. Option 1 or 3 keeps the bright line intact. Which do you want before we answer? **[ANALYSIS: Alex Lee: if option 2, the revenue change for a Rate 5 home converting to a heat pump, using the Rate 5 ResStock homes in `notebooks/eversource_hourly_class_loads.qmd`]**

d. Yes. Rate HP applies to all of the customer's usage in November through March, including electric vehicle charging, as in Massachusetts.[^13d-ma]

   [^13d-ma]: Commonwealth of Massachusetts, _Residential Electric Seasonal Heat Pump Rates_, Mass.gov ("The lower rates apply to all the electricity you use, not just the electricity used by your heat pump") **[NOT INGESTED: inbox `mass_gov_residential_electric_seasonal_heat_pump_rates_capture_20261107.md`; URL and access date TK]**.

   - Rough scale: `{python} est("ev_winter_discount")` a year for a Rate HP customer who also charges an electric vehicle at home.
   - Whether the CIEC-1 figures include this: they apply Rate HP to ResStock's whole-home load **[TK: Alex Lee: does ResStock 2024.2 model EV charging in the Eversource sample? If not, the CIEC-1 figures exclude it]**.
   - Cost causation: winter EV charging, like winter heat pump load, falls in hours with almost no marginal T&D cost (CIEC-9(a)), so at Rate 1's winter rate it would also overpay its incremental cost. The issue is that Rate HP lowers it for heat pump customers only.
   - Charging at peak (summer afternoons) is billed at unchanged Rate 1 rates.
   - Billing heat pump load alone would require a separate meter or circuit-level data the Company does not collect.[^13d-meter]

     [^13d-meter]: CL&P Response to CLF-SC-008, at 1 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; Velez Direct at 81:1–4 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - For the industrial firewall: under the new/existing split, a new heat pump customer's EV discount is part of that customer's bill change, and part (b) applies; an existing customer's is part of the existing-customer shortfall, recovered as described in CIEC-2.
:::

## CIEC-14

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 85, lines 1-19.


a. Please provide the derivation of the 71% winter distribution reduction and the 75% winter transmission reduction, including all inputs and calculations, in Excel format with formulas intact, to the extent not already provided in Exhibit JPV-4 or in response to CIEC-1.
b. Please identify each element of the winter distribution and transmission rates (including any reconciling or rider components) to which the 71% and 75% reductions would apply.
c. Please provide the resulting Rate HP winter rates in cents per kWh for each component.
:::

::: {.response}
a. The derivation is in Exhibit JPV-2, Section 5, and Exhibit JPV-4 **[TK: Alex Lee: confirm JPV-4 has the winter-rate solve with formulas intact; if not, provide it as CIEC-14 Attachment 1 (Google Doc comment 28)]**.

   - Method: for each component, the winter (November–March) rate at which the average fossil fuel-heated customer's post-heat-pump bill equals their pre-heat-pump bill plus the incremental marginal cost of that component.[^14a-method]

     [^14a-method]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 85:2–7 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Formula: winter rate = (bill before + incremental marginal cost − Rate 1 rate × April–October kWh after) ÷ November–March kWh after. The summer rate is held at Rate 1, so the whole correction falls on winter kWh.[^14a-formula]

     [^14a-formula]: Exhibit JPV-2, Section 5.

   - Inputs, average fossil fuel-heated home: `{python} num(r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_before)` kWh a year before and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_annual_kwh_after)` after; November–March usage of `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_winter_before)` kWh before and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_winter_after)` after; April–October usage of `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_summer_before)` before and `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_summer_after)` after; incremental marginal cost of `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_dist_delta, 2)` (distribution) and `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_tx_delta, 2)` (transmission).
   - Results: `{python} cents(hp_winter_dist_ec)` per kWh for the Distribution Energy Charge, down `{python} pct(dist_cut)` from `{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC)`, and `{python} cents(hp_winter_tx)` for the Transmission Service Rate, down `{python} pct(tx_cut)` from `{python} cents(FILED_TX)`.
   - Why the cut is deeper than the rise in winter usage: November–March usage rises `{python} f"{winter_kwh_ratio:.1f}"`-fold, but the rate falls about `{python} f"{breakeven_winter_ratio:.1f}"`-fold. The extra `{python} num(r.all_fossil_kwh_summer_delta)` kWh in April–October (heating in April and October, more cooling in summer) is billed at the unchanged Rate 1 rates, about `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_kwh_summer_delta * FILED_TOTAL_DEL)` a year. The winter rate also has to give that back.
   - Result for the average home: its November–March T&D bill falls from `{python} dollar(winter_bill_before)` to `{python} dollar(winter_bill_after_hp)`, its April–October bill rises by about the same amount, and its annual T&D bill rises by about the `{python} dollar(inc_mc)` of incremental marginal cost.

> **[COUNSEL]** Velez Direct at 85:14–19 says winter usage "roughly quadruples" and that the rate drops "by roughly the same factor." With winter defined as November–March, usage rises about `{python} f"{winter_kwh_ratio:.1f}"`-fold; the rate falls further because of April–October load billed at Rate 1. The rates in Table 4 are unaffected, but the explanation needs an errata or a correction on the stand. (For comparison, National Grid's Massachusetts heat pump rate assumes winter usage 2.8 times the residential average, National Grid Exhibit HP-1 at 4.)

b. The reductions apply to two charges only, in November through March:

   - The Distribution Energy Charge (`{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC)` under proposed Rate 1).
   - The Transmission Service Rate (`{python} cents(FILED_TX)`), set through the Transmission Adjustment Clause.[^14b-tsr]

     [^14b-tsr]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 83:5–8 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - **[TK: JPV: the Transmission Service Rate is reset every May 1 in the annual rate adjustment proceeding (Docket 26-01-03 this year), not in the rate case. Say whether the 75% winter reduction is meant to apply to each year's new rate, which would mean re-deriving it in that proceeding]**

   - They do not apply to the customer charge, generation, or the volumetric riders: the Competitive Transition Assessment, the Systems Benefits Charge, the Conservation Adjustment Mechanism, the Renewable Energy charge and the FMCC Delivery Charge. These net to `{python} cents(FILED_RIDERS)` per kWh and stay at Rate 1 levels.[^14b-riders]

     [^14b-riders]: Velez Direct at 83:1–2, 83 n.74 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Mechanically, the distribution winter rate was solved including the riders, and the riders were then subtracted, so the whole distribution reduction lands on the Distribution Energy Charge.[^14b-mechanics]

     [^14b-mechanics]: Exhibit JPV-2, Section 5.

   - Decoupling is not inside the Distribution Energy Charge: Rate 1 bills a separate decoupling charge per kWh, shown as its own line on the bill.[^14b-rdm] Storm costs are partly inside it: base distribution rates include a reserve funding level for catastrophic storms, with costs above it recovered through a separate storm charge.[^14b-storm] The tariff does not say how much of the 12.196¢ that reserve represents.

     [^14b-rdm]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-3 at 244 (Rate 1, "REVENUE DECOUPLING MECHANISM"), 404 (the RDM charge appears "as a line item under the Local Delivery Detail category") (July 14, 2026) [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

     [^14b-storm]: _Id._ at 427 (base distribution rates include "annual recovery for catastrophic storm costs") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026h].

c. Rate HP rates, winter (November–March), against proposed Rate 1:

   - Distribution Energy Charge: `{python} cents(hp_winter_dist_ec)` per kWh (Rate 1: `{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC)`).
   - Transmission Service Rate: `{python} cents(hp_winter_tx)` (Rate 1: `{python} cents(FILED_TX)`).
   - Riders, net: `{python} cents(FILED_RIDERS)`, unchanged.
   - Total delivery volumetric rate: `{python} cents(hp_winter_total)` (Rate 1: `{python} cents(FILED_TOTAL_DEL)`), down `{python} pct(1 - hp_winter_total / FILED_TOTAL_DEL)`.
   - Summer (April–October) rates, the customer charge of `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, 2)` a month, and generation: identical to Rate 1.[^14c-same]

     [^14c-same]: Velez Direct at 82:10–83:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - These are computed at the Company's filed Rate 1 values and would be recomputed from the rates the Authority approves (CIEC-9(c)).

## CIEC-15

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 97, lines 3-13, and page 98, lines 1-18.


a. Please provide the derivation of the $121.49 monthly customer charge, in Excel format with formulas intact, to the extent not already provided in Exhibit JPV-2, Section 6.
b. Please design, or describe the design of, a heat pump rate that would eliminate the overpayment Mr. Velez identifies while remaining revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole, and provide the resulting rates.
c. If Mr. Velez contends that no such rate is feasible, please explain why.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Exhibit JPV-2, Section 6 gives the full derivation.[^15a-n85] An Excel version is provided as CIEC-15 Attachment 1 **[TK: Alex Lee: does a workbook exist (Google Doc comment 31)? If not, build it from `notebooks/incremental_fair_default.qmd`]**. In brief:

   [^15a-n85]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 97 n.85 (Oct. 21, 2026) [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Step 1: find the factor by which Rate 1's distribution and transmission volumetric rates would have to be scaled so that the representative home's increase in those charges after installing a heat pump equals its incremental marginal T&D cost, `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_marginal_cost, 2)` a year. The factor is `{python} pct(fc.implied_lambda, 1)`: the rates would be cut by `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)`.
   - Step 2: hold the residential class's revenue constant. The two charges collect about `{python} dollar(fc.class_variable_revenue_per_customer)` per residential customer a year at filed rates, across `{python} num(fc.class_customers)` customers. Cutting them by `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)` leaves `{python} million(fc.class_revenue_shift, 0)` a year to recover through the customer charge.
   - Result: the customer charge rises by `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge_delta, 2)`, from `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, 2)` to `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, 2)` a month.

b. Rate HP, with Rate 1 set in the same rate case to recover the residential revenue requirement net of Rate HP revenue, is such a design. The residential class recovers the same T&D revenue requirement with or without Rate HP.

> **[COUNSEL]** The testimony does not say in so many words that Rate 1 is set to recover the remainder; it says Rate HP should be recalibrated in later rate cases (Velez Direct at 7:9–12) and describes a "tech-specific rate" as having a lever that "any rate that must be revenue neutral with respect to the residential class as a whole" lacks (98:10–12). This response, CIEC-1(a) and CIEC-2(c) state it as Mr. Velez's recommendation. The Company itself treats Rates 1 and 7 as one revenue class and Rate 5 as another (CL&P Response to CLF-SC-035, at 1; Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-2.1), so "the residential class" should read "Rate 1 and Rate 7" or "the residential classes" where precision matters. Rate HP is built on Rate 1, so it would sit in the Rate 1 and 7 revenue class. **[TK: JPV: how to treat Rate 5 heat pump customers who enroll in Rate HP; their move shifts revenue from the Rate 5 class to the Rate 1 and 7 class, and Rate 5 is not mentioned in the testimony's recovery recommendation]**

   - Any rate that eliminates the overpayment must collect less from heat pump customers than Rate 1 does, because the overpayment is the amount Rate 1 collects above each customer's pre-heat-pump bill plus incremental marginal cost.
   - New heat pump customers: collecting less from them than Rate 1 would requires nothing from anyone else. They still pay more than they did before installing, so no part of the residential revenue requirement goes unrecovered.
   - Existing heat pump customers: collecting less from them than Rate 1 does creates the shortfall in CIEC-1(a). Recalibrating Rate 1 recovers it from the rest of the residential class.
   - Resulting rates, November through March: Rate HP distribution energy charge `{python} cents(hp_winter_dist_ec)` per kWh and Transmission Service Rate `{python} cents(hp_winter_tx)` per kWh. Summer rates, riders, generation and the customer charge are those of Rate 1.[^15b-same]

     [^15b-same]: [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 82:10–83:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Resulting Rate 1 rates, if existing heat pump customers are auto-enrolled: distribution energy charge `{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC + c3.floor_per_kwh['dist'])` to `{python} cents(FILED_DIST_EC + c3.ceiling_per_kwh['dist'])` per kWh, and Transmission Service Rate `{python} cents(FILED_TX + c3.floor_per_kwh['tx'])` to `{python} cents(FILED_TX + c3.ceiling_per_kwh['tx'])` per kWh, at the floor and ceiling enrollment estimates (CIEC-3(c)). If only new heat pump customers enroll, Rate 1 is unchanged.
   - The passage CIEC cites describes a single rate schedule, not the class:[^15b-passage] a default rate, or any rate that must recover the class's revenue on its own, cannot lower volumetric charges without raising something else. A heat pump rate can lower charges for its own customers because Rate 1 is set to recover the remainder.

     [^15b-passage]: Velez Direct at 98:10–12 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - A second design keeps a single schedule and is also revenue neutral for the class: the Rate 1 redesign in part (a), with volumetric T&D rates at `{python} pct(fc.implied_lambda, 1)` of filed levels and a `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, 2)` monthly customer charge. The testimony does not recommend it because it would change every residential bill and would be regressive without income-graduated charges.[^15b-regressive]

     [^15b-regressive]: Velez Direct at 97:14–16 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

c. Not applicable: such a rate is feasible (part (b)).

   - What is not feasible is a heat pump rate that eliminates the overpayment while collecting the same revenue from heat pump customers as Rate 1. Raising summer rates to make up for lower winter rates only moves the overpayment between seasons (CIEC-3(a)).[^15c-shift]

     [^15c-shift]: Velez Direct at 101:7–10 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

:::

## CIEC-16

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 5, lines 10-13, and page 30, lines 9-17.


a. Please confirm that the cross-subsidy Mr. Velez identifies is a cross-subsidy within the residential class.
b. Please explain why any revenue reduction resulting from a remedy for a cross-subsidy within the residential class should, or should not, be borne by customers outside the residential class.
:::

::: {.response}
a. Confirmed. As rates are set, the cross-subsidy runs within the residential class, from customers who heat with heat pumps to those who heat with fossil fuels.[^16a-within]

   [^16a-within]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 5:12–13 (Oct. 21, 2026) (the cross-subsidy runs "from electric customers that heat with heat pumps to those that heat with fossil fuels") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - One qualification, between rate cases: when heat pump load grows faster than the Company forecast, the extra Rate 1 revenue (including the overpayment on it) is returned to all classes through the Revenue Decoupling Mechanism, at a flat rate per kWh.[^16a-rdm] Part of the overpayment therefore reaches non-residential customers until the next rate case (CIEC-2(d)).

     [^16a-rdm]: Joint Direct Testimony of Edward Davis and Kimberly R. Parsons on behalf of The Connecticut Light and Power Company d/b/a Eversource Energy ("Davis-Parsons Direct"), Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 22:21 (July 14, 2026) ("the rate will be set at a flat kWh rate across all rate classes") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f] **[TK: no public copy to link yet]**.

b. It should not be borne by customers outside the residential class.

   - The remedy returns money to where it came from. The overpayment is collected from residential heat pump customers and lowers rates for residential fossil fuel-heated customers; ending it should raise those customers' rates, not anyone else's.
   - The cross-subsidy is a problem of rate design within the class, not of the class's share of the revenue requirement. The class revenue allocation determines each class's share, and Rate HP leaves it unchanged; no other class's cost of service changes.
   - Only one part of the remedy reduces revenue: _existing_ heat pump customers moving to Rate HP. _New_ heat pump customers reduce no one's revenue (CIEC-12(a)). So the only amount to which this question applies is the existing-customer reduction, `{python} million(short_floor['total'])` to `{python} million(short_ceiling['total'])` a year (CIEC-12(c)).
   - Mr. Velez recommends recovering that amount within the residential class, in this rate case and between rate cases (CIEC-2(c) and (d)).
   - Mr. Velez has found no Authority decision on remedying a cross-subsidy within a class. The closest precedents keep residential costs mostly within the residential class:
     - Within the class: in UI's 2023 rate case, the Authority applied the residential classes' revenue reduction from a lower customer charge to residential usage rates.[^16b-ui]

       [^16b-ui]: Docket No. 22-08-08, _Application of The United Illuminating Company to Amend Its Rate Schedule_, [Decision](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/dockcurr.nsf/4b3c728dd1c0d642852586db0069aa70/dd7c1a0c81056b1485258a16004f1d22/%24FILE/220808-082523.pdf), at 237, 242 (Aug. 25, 2023) ("the reduction to the class revenue requirement for Rates R and RT due to the reduction in the customer charge shall be applied to usage rates") **[NOT INGESTED]**.

     - Mostly within the class, for now: the residential low-income discount rate's costs are recovered through the Systems Benefits Charge, and the Authority left the class allocation of those costs to rate cases.[^16b-lidr] The Company's Systems Benefits Charge assigns costs to the class that incurred them,[^16b-sbc-tracked] which is why the residential charge is several times the commercial and industrial charges.[^16b-sbc-rates] **[UNVERIFIED IDEA: no document says outright that the discount dollars are tracked to the residential classes; that is the implication of the method]**

       [^16b-lidr]: Docket No. 17-12-03RE11, _PURA Investigation into Distribution System Planning of the Electric Distribution Companies – New Rate Designs and Rates Review_, [Decision](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/2nddockcurr.nsf/8e6fc37a54110e3e852576190052b64d/cd198950921e4b93852588e000512853/%24FILE/171203RE11-101922.pdf), at 29 ("All costs shall be reconciled through the SBC"), 30 ("With respect to the cost allocation methodology among rate classes through the SBC, the Authority concludes there is insufficient record evidence to date, and that cost allocation is more appropriately considered within the broader context of a rate case proceeding.") (Oct. 19, 2022) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

       [^16b-sbc-tracked]: Docket No. 23-01-03, _PURA Annual Review of the Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company_, [Decision](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/dockcurr.nsf/4b3c728dd1c0d642852586db0069aa70/2458b17f1ae4f1de85258a0d00503765/%24FILE/230103-081623.pdf), at 29 (Aug. 16, 2023) (the Company "pro-rates the SBC costs across rate classes using the prior year actual SBC costs that are tracked under each individual rate class, which ties the costs incurred for the SBC programs to be recouped by the same rate class of customers who generated the costs initially") **[NOT INGESTED]**.

       [^16b-sbc-rates]: Docket No. 26-01-03, CL&P Annual Rate Adjustment Mechanism Filing, Exhibit C, line 22 (Mar. 2, 2026) (Systems Benefits Charge of 1.587¢ per kWh for residential, 0.346¢ for commercial and 0.329¢ for industrial customers, for rates effective January 1, 2026) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

     - That may change. In December 2025 the Authority called the disparity "inequitable" and tentatively adopted an energy allocator for the Company's Systems Benefits Charge, which the Company estimated would lower residential rates and raise commercial and industrial rates by about 1¢ per kWh.[^16b-sbc-2025] **[TK: whether the energy allocator took effect; neither the 26-01-03 decision nor the March 2026 filing mentions it]**

       [^16b-sbc-2025]: Docket No. 24-12-05, _PURA Procedural Review of the Annual Rate Adjustment Mechanisms of The Connecticut Light and Power Company and The United Illuminating Company_, [Decision](https://www.dpuc.state.ct.us/dockcurr.nsf/4b3c728dd1c0d642852586db0069aa70/27c546791b13210c85258d5c00529872/%24FILE/241205-121025.pdf), at 18 ("specific to Eversource, the Authority tentatively adopts an energy allocator for the SBC"), 19 ("residential rate classes would reduce by approximately 1 cent/kWh and commercial and industrial customers would subsequently increase approximately 1 cent/kWh"), 20 ("This disparity is inequitable") (Dec. 10, 2025) **[NOT INGESTED]**.

     - Even if it does, the low-income discount is a public-policy program; Rate HP corrects a cost-of-service problem within one class, so the within-class treatment is the closer analogy.
   - The Company applies the same principle to its own residential rate designs: Rate 6 ensures no harm to other classes, and a winter transmission discount would be made up within the class.[^16b-company] Massachusetts found its heat pump rates would not raise costs for other customers.[^16b-ma]

     [^16b-company]: Davis-Parsons Direct, Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 37:18 (Rate 6 "Ensures no incremental harm to remaining customer classes") [@clp_Docket260510Exhibit_2026f]; [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-032](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a), at 1 (a winter discount would be offset "to meet total transmission revenue requirements for the class") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026a].

     [^16b-ma]: D.P.U. 25-08-A, Order on Seasonal Heat Pump Rates, at 20 (June 1, 2026) (the rates "will not increase costs to other customers beyond the cost to serve those customers") [@madpu_Docket2508Order_2026] **[TK: case caption; no public copy to link yet]**.

   - The Authority has said it is inclined to make the decoupling mechanism better reflect cost causation across classes,[^16b-rdm-2023] though in 2025 it kept the company-wide kWh allocator for now (CIEC-2(d)).

     [^16b-rdm-2023]: Docket No. 23-01-03 Decision at 30 (the RDM should "better reflect the underlying cost causation principles relied upon to allocate base distribution costs amongst customers classes") **[NOT INGESTED]**.

:::

## CIEC-17

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 100, lines 11-13.


a. Please explain what Mr. Velez means by pricing incremental heat pump loads at “(closer to)” marginal cost, and state whether he believes incremental heat pump load should make any contribution to the recovery of embedded T&D costs.
b. If Mr. Velez believes incremental heat pump load should make some contribution to embedded T&D costs, please quantify the contribution reflected in Rate HP.
:::

::: {.response}
a. "(Closer to)" means that Rate HP prices the average customer's incremental heat pump load at about its incremental marginal cost, not exactly at it, for each customer. Incremental heat pump load should not add to the customer's contribution to embedded T&D costs. The customer's pre-heat-pump contribution is kept.

   - The phrase describes an objective the testimony shares with the Company.[^17a-objective] The Company sets the floor for its Rate 6 discount at the incremental cost of the converting customer's added load.[^17a-floor]

     [^17a-objective]: [Direct Testimony of Juan-Pablo Velez on behalf of Conservation Law Foundation and Sierra Club](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) ("Velez Direct"), at 100:12 (Oct. 21, 2026) ("I share the Company’s objective of pricing incremental heat pump loads at (closer to) marginal cost") [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

     [^17a-floor]: [CL&P Response to CLF-003(b)](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026), at 1–2 ("The discounted rate is set to cover the incremental cost of serving the additional load the converting customer adds, which establishes the floor") [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026]; _see also_ [Velez Direct](https://pub.switch.box/velez_Docket260510Direct_2026) at 26:9–11 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - "Closer to," because a single winter rate applies to all of a customer's winter usage, not only to the heat pump's share of it. Rate HP is calibrated so that the population-average T&D bill equals the pre-heat-pump bill plus incremental marginal cost.[^17a-calibrated] Individual customers still over- or underpay.[^17a-individual]

     [^17a-calibrated]: Velez Direct at 85:2–7 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

     [^17a-individual]: Velez Direct at 85:8–10 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Under Rate HP, the mean overpayment is `{python} dollar(op.overpay_mean_fair_seasonal_rate_all_fossil, 2)` a year, and `{python} pct(op.pct_within_200_seasonal)` of fossil fuel-heated homes that switch fall within \$200 of zero.[^17a-distribution]

     [^17a-distribution]: Velez Direct at 86:13–14, 88:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Pricing incremental load exactly at marginal cost would take a per-customer threshold set at each customer's pre-heat-pump usage.[^17a-threshold] The Company does not have interval meters, so it would need new billing software or circuit-level monitors installed with each heat pump (CIEC-13(d)).[^17a-meters]

     [^17a-threshold]: Velez Direct at 86:3–4 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

     [^17a-meters]: [CL&P Response to CLF-SC-008](https://pub.switch.box/clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b), at 1 [@clp_Docket260510Responses_2026b]; Velez Direct at 81:1–4 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - On embedded costs: Rate HP is designed to keep the revenue the Company collected from each customer's base load.[^17a-base-load] So heat pump customers keep contributing to embedded costs what they contributed before installing. Their incremental load adds nothing beyond its marginal cost, because embedded costs are sunk, and charging new load for them would be a charge for costs that load did not cause.[^17a-sunk]

     [^17a-base-load]: Velez Direct at 81:18–21 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

     [^17a-sunk]: Velez Direct at 13:23–14:2 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - The Company's proposed Economic Development Rate uses the same principle for large commercial and industrial expansion load: a minimum charge anchored to marginal cost (CIEC-5(c)).

b. Rate HP keeps the representative customer's pre-heat-pump contribution to embedded T&D costs, about `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` a year,[^17b-pre] and adds about `{python} dollar(op.overpay_mean_fair_seasonal_rate_all_fossil)` from incremental load, on average, for a total of about `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate_hp)` a year.[^17b-total]

   [^17b-pre]: `{python} dollar(pre_td)` in pre-heat-pump T&D charges minus `{python} dollar(pre_mc)` in marginal T&D cost (CIEC-4(a)).

   [^17b-total]: `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` plus the mean overpayment under Rate HP, `{python} dollar(op.overpay_mean_fair_seasonal_rate_all_fossil, 2)`. Velez Direct at 86:13–14 [@velez_Docket260510Direct_2026].

   - Under Rate 1, the same customer would contribute about `{python} dollar(embedded_after_rate1)` a year after installing (CIEC-4(b)).
   - New heat pump customers: the `{python} dollar(embedded_gap)` is what they already paid before installing, so their contribution is unchanged.
   - Existing heat pump customers: they take the same rates, so their contribution is set the same way, on average. Their bills fall `{python} dollar(c1.dec_total, 2)` a year below Rate 1 (CIEC-1(a)), and that difference is the shortfall recovered on Rate 1.
:::

## CIEC-19

::: {.question}
Please refer to Velez Direct Testimony at page 58, lines 11-19, and footnotes 60 and 61.


a. Please identify each portion of Velez Direct Testimony in which Mr. Velez relies on the RAP Cost Allocation Manual, and state the proposition for which he relies on it in each instance.
b. Please state whether Mr. Velez is aware of any criticism or rebuttal of the RAP Cost Allocation Manual’s recommendations that has been presented in testimony, reports or other publications, and identify any such materials he has reviewed.
c. Please describe Mr. Velez’s understanding of whether the RAP Cost Allocation Manual was subject to peer review, or to review by utility, industrial customer or other stakeholder representatives, before publication.
d. Please identify each proceeding in which Mr. Velez or Switchbox has cited the RAP Cost Allocation Manual in testimony, reports or comments, and state the outcome on the issue for which it was cited.
:::

::: {.response}
**[COUNSEL: same burden objection as CIEC-18 for part (b), limited to materials Mr. Velez has reviewed]**

a. Two places:

   - Page 58, lines 11–19, and footnotes 60–61: when regulators treat new and existing loads differently, they should make sure the distinction is not arbitrary and rests on solid reasoning, and the Manual's examples of legitimate differential treatment involve new loads that impose different costs.[^19a-58] The testimony uses this to argue that Rate 6's cutoff by installation date is arbitrary, because heat pump customers on either side of it receive the same service at the same marginal cost.[^19a-cutoff]

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** CIEC-12, 18 and 19 point at a tension CIEC may exploit. At 58:8–19 the testimony says treating pre- and post-2026 heat pump customers differently is arbitrary, because their costs are the same. These responses say, over and over, that new and existing customers have very different effects on revenue. Both are true, and they are consistent, but the response should say why: Rate HP charges new and existing heat pump customers the _same_ rate, because their costs are the same; the difference is only in what happens to the Company's revenue when each moves to that rate, because existing customers' load is already in the sales used to set Rate 1. Rate 6 excludes existing customers from the rate altogether, which keeps the revenue effect at zero but leaves them overpaying. Suggest adding one bullet to CIEC-12 making this explicit, and not saying more here. CIEC may also point to the Company's Economic Development Rate, which excludes existing load "consistent with prior regulatory determinations" (Exhibit CLP-RATES-1 at 25:6–7); the difference is that the EDR is a discount below class rates for load growth, while Rate HP corrects an overcharge on load that is already there. **[UNVERIFIED IDEA]** that this is what CIEC is setting up.

> **[DISCUSSION FOR JPV]** The Oregon order (UM 2377, Order No. 26-154) was not in my search; RAP sent it to you on Nov. 9. I read it and revised (a)–(e) above. Four things to note. (1) The order does not name the Manual: it says "a report by RAP" submitted through CUB's testimony. I pulled that testimony (CUB/300, Jenks surrebuttal, Dec. 19, 2025) from the UM 2377 docket and read it: at Jenks/15–16 it quotes the Manual on loss-of-energy expectation (citing CUB/116 at 56, which is the Manual's p. 54), reproduces the Manual's table of generation demand allocation options, and asks the Commission to require PGE to study those four approaches. CUB's opening testimony lists CUB/116 as the Manual. So the identification is solid, though it runs through CUB's testimony and not the order's text. CUB's pin to "134" is one PDF page off from Table 22 in our copy. (2) This changes my earlier "None" in (c): in both Colorado and Oregon the Manual figured in a directive to study further, and I rewrote (c) to say so. The Colorado ¶ 54 point already made "None" vulnerable. (3) Oregon is also useful beyond this question: the Commission adopted a growth-based allocator (the Peak Growth Modifier) because data centers drive incremental costs, which is the kind of differential treatment the Manual's §6.3 and Ch. 16 describe, and which Velez 58:11–19 says needs a cost basis. But the order does not cite the Manual for that, so I did not say it did. It bears on the CIEC-12/19 tension flagged under CIEC-19: Oregon shows differential treatment is accepted where the new load causes different costs, and Velez's point is that heat pump customers on either side of the Rate 6 cutoff do not. (4) PGE opposed the study in Oregon on grounds of delay and because its own analysis gave higher residential allocations; that is not criticism of the Manual, so I left it out of CIEC-19(b). Add Attachment 2 (Order No. 26-154 at 16–20, 33–34, plus the caption page) to the attachment list, and ingest the order (saved to the inbox) so the **[NOT INGESTED]** flags can be replaced with links.
